recall_basic.q: Who is the only person who can legally obligate the Government on a contract?
recall_basic.a: The contracting officer (CO), through a warrant.
d: The program manager, once funds are certified.
Any Government employee with express or implied authority.
The squadron or unit commander, within command authority.
recall_basic.x: Authority is the whole ballgame: PMs own requirements, commanders own missions, FM owns funds — but none of them can obligate the Government. Only a CO, acting inside a written warrant, binds the United States. Every unauthorized-commitment mess starts with someone forgetting this.

recall_basic.q: Your real value as a 1102 isn't running the package — it's what?
recall_basic.a: Business judgment — sound, defensible decisions.
d: Processing speed — getting actions on contract fast.
Regulatory recall — citing the right rule from memory.
Customer service — giving the program what it asks for.
recall_basic.x: The package is the artifact, not the product. What senior leaders and mission partners actually need from you is a defensible business decision — strategy, competition, fair price, managed risk. If you optimize for processing speed or customer appeasement, you produce fast, indefensible actions.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: Can a COR change a contract's price, scope, or terms?
recall_basic.a: No — only the CO can.
d: Yes — that's the COR's core function.
Yes, but only within the contract's existing ceiling.
Only with the program manager's written concurrence.
recall_basic.x: The COR is the CO's eyes on performance — nothing more. A COR who adjusts price, scope, or terms (or tells the contractor to start something new) is making an unauthorized commitment. All contractual direction flows through the CO; everyone else talks technically.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: Who certifies that funds are available?
recall_basic.a: Financial Management (FM / Comptroller).
d: The contracting officer, when signing the award.
The program manager, as owner of the requirement.
The Judge Advocate (JA), during legal review.
recall_basic.x: Funds certification is FM/Comptroller's lane — the CO can't self-certify money, and the PM owning the budget isn't certification. No certified funds, no award: it's why the money check happens early, not at signature.

recall_basic.q: What document makes someone a CO?
recall_basic.a: A written warrant (SF 1402).
d: A letter of delegation from the program manager.
A COR designation letter.
Their position description and grade (GS-1102).
recall_basic.x: The warrant (SF 1402) is the written delegation that creates contracting authority — position, grade, and job title create none. That's also the audit trail: when someone claims authority, the first question is 'show me the warrant and its limits.'

recall_basic.q: Someone without authority tells a contractor to start work — what is that, and is the Government bound?
recall_basic.a: An unauthorized commitment (UAC); not bound unless it's ratified.
d: A constructive change; the Government is bound once work starts.
An implied contract; binding if the contractor acted in good faith.
A letter contract; binding up to 50% of the estimated value.
recall_basic.x: No authority, no contract — the Government isn't bound, but the contractor performed in good faith, so you have a UAC to fix. Ratification (an official with actual authority approving it after the fact) is the documented exception, never the routine. A constructive change requires an existing contract; a UAC has none.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: What's the governing rulebook now, and what's being retired?
recall_basic.a: The RFO and R-DFARS; the legacy FAR / DFARS / DAFFARS.
d: The legacy FAR and DFARS; the RFO pilot program.
The DAF Contracting Compass; the RFO and R-DFARS.
Title 10 procedures; the FAR and all agency supplements.
recall_basic.x: Under E.O. 14275 the RFO replaces the legacy FAR, and DoD's supplement is being reissued as the R-DFARS through class deviations. Citing legacy FAR/DFARS/DAFFARS in a new action tells a reviewer your references are stale.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: Where do you confirm a current threshold or rule?
recall_basic.a: acquisition.gov/far-overhaul — never quote from memory.
d: The most recent printed FAR edition in the office.
The DAU threshold poster — updated each fiscal year.
Your training notes — thresholds change only with the NDAA.
recall_basic.x: The rules are mid-rewrite: content is moving, renumbering, and thresholds shifted in 2025–2026. Printed guides, posters, and memory all rot — the live RFO text and current class deviations at acquisition.gov/far-overhaul are the only safe confirmation.

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: Name the three-part fiscal test.
recall_basic.a: Time · Purpose · Amount (TPA).
d: Color · Ceiling · Currency (CCC).
Need · Funds · Approval (NFA).
Obligate · Expend · Close out (OEC).
recall_basic.x: Time (right period, bona fide need), Purpose (what Congress appropriated it for), Amount (no more than available — the ADA line). Every fiscal question you'll ever get is one of these three wearing a costume.
recall_basic.ref: Field Guide Vol. 1 §5 · GAO Red Book

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: Can you use this year's money for next year's need?
recall_basic.a: Generally no — the bona fide need rule.
d: Yes, if the funds are obligated before 30 September.
Yes — appropriations are interchangeable within DoD.
Only with an approved Anti-Deficiency Act waiver.
recall_basic.x: Appropriations serve the needs of their own period — that's the bona fide need rule, and it's Time in the T-P-A test. Obligating this year's money for next year's need doesn't become legal by rushing it before 30 September; that timing move is the classic violation, not the cure.
recall_basic.ref: Field Guide Vol. 1 §5 · GAO Red Book

recall_basic.q: What runs underneath every phase of the lifecycle?
recall_basic.a: The contract file / documentation (and oversight).
d: The source selection plan and evaluation criteria.
The program's budget and spend plan.
Contractor performance surveillance by the COR.
recall_basic.x: Phases change; the file doesn't. Documentation and oversight run under every phase because each decision must survive an auditor, an IG, and a protest — sometimes years later, argued by people who weren't in the room.

recall_basic.q: If it isn't in the file…
recall_basic.a: …it didn't happen. The file tells the story of every decision.
d: …email records can substitute at audit.
…the CO's memory of the decision controls.
…it can be reconstructed after award without issue.
recall_basic.x: Memory doesn't testify and emails scatter — the contract file is the single record that tells the story of why each decision was made. If a decision isn't documented there, for review purposes it didn't happen.

recall_basic.q: What does market research tell you?
recall_basic.a: Who can perform, whether it's commercial, whether small businesses can compete, and a realistic price.
d: Which vendor the program should select and at what price.
Whether the requirement is funded with the right color of money.
The evaluation factors and their relative importance.
recall_basic.x: Market research answers the four strategy-driving questions: who can perform, is it commercial, can small business compete, and what's a realistic price. It doesn't pick your vendor (that's the competition's job) and it doesn't touch the funding question (that's FM's).

recall_basic.q: What's the Government's own price estimate called?
recall_basic.a: The IGCE (Independent Government Cost Estimate).
d: The should-cost baseline (SCB).
The program office estimate of record (POE).
The budgetary rough order of magnitude (B-ROM).
recall_basic.x: The IGCE is the Government's own independent estimate — your pre-negotiation yardstick for price reasonableness and your reality check on quotes. Push for one on every real buy; you can't judge a price with nothing to judge it against.

recall_basic.q: What's the default for buys over the SAT ($350K)?
recall_basic.a: Full and open competition.
d: Small business set-aside under the Rule of Two.
Simplified acquisition procedures with three quotes.
Whatever method market research recommends.
recall_basic.x: CICA makes full and open competition the statutory default over the SAT. Set-asides and sole source are exceptions that must be earned — by the Rule of Two being met, or by a documented RFO 6.103 exception. The default never needs justifying; departures do.

recall_basic.q: If you can't compete it, what do you need?
recall_basic.a: A justification (J&A) under a recognized exception.
d: A Determination & Findings (D&F) signed by the PM.
Written sole-source approval from the requiring activity.
A memo for record explaining the urgency.
recall_basic.x: Other than full and open competition takes a Justification & Approval citing one of the seven recognized exceptions, approved at the right dollar tier. A D&F is a different instrument, a PM can't approve away competition, and a memo isn't a J&A.

recall_basic.q: Micro-purchase threshold?
recall_basic.x: $15,000 since the 1 October 2025 adjustment — $10K is the legacy figure people still quote from old guides, and $3,500 is ancient history. Below the MPT you're usually on the GPC, with fair distribution among sources but no formal competition file.

recall_basic.q: Simplified Acquisition Threshold (SAT)?
recall_basic.x: $350,000 since 1 October 2025 — $250K is the pre-adjustment number your instincts may still carry. The SAT is the biggest fork in the road: above it, full CICA and formal procedures; below it, SAP with the small-business reservation.

recall_basic.q: On a firm-fixed-price contract, who bears the cost risk?
recall_basic.a: The contractor.
d: The Government.
Both parties, split by the share ratio.
Neither — cost risk applies only to cost-type contracts.
recall_basic.x: FFP means one price, whatever it actually costs — the contractor owns every dollar of cost risk, which is why it fits well-defined, priceable work. The share-ratio answer describes incentive contracts (FPIF/CPIF), not firm-fixed-price.

recall_basic.q: When is a cost-type contract appropriate?
recall_basic.a: When the work is too uncertain to price firmly (e.g., R&D).
d: When the Government wants the strongest incentive for cost control.
When the requirement is commercial and well-defined.
Whenever the contractor's proposed price exceeds the IGCE.
recall_basic.x: Cost-type is the honest answer when nobody can price the work — R&D, novel development. It's not a reward for weak proposals and not a cost-control tool; the Government takes the cost risk precisely because the uncertainty is real. Forcing FFP there just buys a padded price.

recall_basic.q: What's the goal of price analysis, and is it always required?
recall_basic.a: A fair and reasonable price — and yes, always.
d: The lowest possible price — only on competitive buys.
Cost realism — only on cost-type contracts.
A fair and reasonable price — but only above the SAT.
recall_basic.x: Every action — every dollar value, every method — requires a documented conclusion that the price is fair and reasonable. Competition is the best evidence, but even a $50 GPC buy rides on a judgment. 'Always' is the load-bearing word the distractors chip at.

recall_basic.q: Mod adds $1M and deletes $1M — what value counts for the certified-data threshold?
recall_basic.a: $2M (absolute value of each, not the net).
d: $0 — additions and deletions net against each other.
$1M — the larger single change controls.
The full contract value, remeasured after the mod.
recall_basic.x: For the certified-data threshold, additions and deletions each count at absolute value — $1M added plus $1M deleted is a $2M pricing action, not zero. Netting them out is the classic dodge the rule is written to defeat: both sides of the change get priced.

recall_basic.q: Section L vs. Section M?
recall_basic.a: L = how to submit; M = how you'll be evaluated.
d: L = the evaluation factors; M = the proposal instructions.
L = the labor requirements; M = the milestone schedule.
L = terms for large business; M = terms for small business.
recall_basic.x: Section L instructs offerors how to prepare and submit; Section M tells them how you'll evaluate. They must trace perfectly — asking for something L-side that M never evaluates (or evaluating what you never asked for) is the flaw protesters hunt first.

recall_basic.q: What is "best value"?
recall_basic.a: The best mix of price and non-price factors for the Government.
d: The lowest-priced technically acceptable offer, always.
The highest-rated technical proposal regardless of price.
The offer closest to the Government's own estimate.
recall_basic.x: Best value is the best mix of price and non-price factors for the Government — a continuum from LPTA (cheapest acceptable) to tradeoff (paying more when it's worth it). It's never 'cheapest, period' or 'best technical regardless of price'; those are its two failure modes.

recall_basic.q: What are you protecting during a source selection?
recall_basic.a: Source-selection information and contractor proposal data (the PIA).
d: Classified and controlled unclassified information (CUI).
The contract file and past-performance records (CPARS).
Personally identifiable information (PII) under the Privacy Act.
recall_basic.x: The PIA protects two things: the Government's source selection information (rankings, evaluations, the estimate) and the offerors' proprietary bid/proposal data. CUI and PII matter under other regimes — the PIA is specifically about competition-sensitive information.

recall_basic.q: You spot an integrity problem — first move?
recall_basic.a: Stop, and call your CO and JA (legal) immediately.
d: Quietly correct it and document what you did.
Report it to the contractor's ethics office first.
Finish the evaluation, then raise it at award review.
recall_basic.x: Integrity problems compound with handling: quietly fixing it destroys evidence, and waiting until award review lets taint spread. Stop, preserve, and call the CO and JA the same day — a 5-minute call is recoverable; a helpful cover-up rarely is.

recall_basic.q: State the Rule of Two.
recall_basic.a: Set it aside if you expect two or more small businesses to compete at fair market prices.
d: Get at least two quotes on every buy above the MPT.
Two responsible sources must exist before any competition.
Award to small business when at least two respond to the synopsis.
recall_basic.x: The Rule of Two runs on reasonable expectation at strategy time — two or more capable small businesses likely to offer at fair market prices → set it aside. It isn't a quote-count mandate and it isn't judged by who ultimately shows up; that's why the research documentation matters.

recall_basic.q: What drives the small-business size standard?
recall_basic.a: The NAICS code you assign.
d: The contract's total dollar value.
The firm's SAM.gov registration category.
The PSC (product service code) on the requirement.
recall_basic.x: The NAICS code you assign sets the size standard — who counts as 'small' for this buy. Wrong code, wrong universe of eligible firms, wrong set-aside analysis, and a size-protest headache. Dollar value and SAM categories don't decide it; your code does.
recall_basic.ref: Field Guide Vol. 1 §14 · SBA size standards

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: Who watches contractor performance day-to-day?
recall_basic.a: The COR — but only the CO changes the deal.
d: The CO personally — surveillance can't be delegated.
The program manager, as owner of the requirement.
DCMA, on every contract regardless of assignment.
recall_basic.x: Day-to-day surveillance belongs to the COR; deal-changing belongs to the CO — that split is the whole design. DCMA administers only assigned contracts, and the PM watching the mission isn't contract surveillance. When those lanes blur, constructive changes and UACs follow.

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: A change so big it goes beyond the original contract's scope is a…?
recall_basic.a: Cardinal change — it needs new competition or a J&A, not a modification.
d: Constructive change — compensable through an equitable adjustment.
Major modification — allowed with one-level-up approval.
Supplemental agreement — valid once both parties sign.
recall_basic.x: A cardinal change is work so far beyond the original competition that the Changes clause can't authorize it — effectively a new procurement (and potentially a breach). The fix is competition or a J&A, not a signature: even a bilateral mod can't launder new work into an old contract.

recall_basic.q: The four values that anchor every contract action?
recall_basic.a: Stewardship · mission · integrity · documentation.
d: Speed · savings · satisfaction · safety.
Competition · compliance · courtesy · closure.
Authority · funding · fairness · files.
recall_basic.x: The guide anchors every action on stewardship (public money), mission (speed matters), integrity (competition and fairness), and documentation (the file tells the story). Each pillar answers a different overseer: the auditor, the warfighter, the public, and the protest.

recall_basic.q: Every action you take should survive which three reviewers?
recall_basic.a: An auditor, an Inspector General, and a protest.
d: The PM, the commander, and the customer.
DCMA, DCAA, and GSA.
The SSA, the SSEB, and the ombudsman.
recall_basic.x: Auditor, IG, protest — the three reviewers who will read your file years later without you in the room. Writing for them now is what 'defensible' means; the PM and commander read for mission, not for compliance.

recall_basic.q: Is "because the program wanted it" ever a complete answer?
recall_basic.a: Never — the file needs the business judgment behind the decision.
d: Yes, when the program certifies the funds.
Yes — the requiring activity owns the requirement.
Only above the SAT does the file need more.
recall_basic.x: The program's desire is an input, never the justification. The file needs the business judgment — market facts, price analysis, competition rationale. Fund certification and requirement ownership don't substitute for the why.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: PCO vs. ACO — who's who?
recall_basic.a: PCO awards and manages the contract; the ACO (often DCMA) handles post-award administration.
d: PCO handles post-award administration; the ACO awards.
PCO is the specialist; the ACO holds the warrant.
They're the same officer at different dollar values.
recall_basic.x: The PCO awards and manages; the ACO — usually at DCMA — carries assigned post-award administration like payments, mods, and monitoring. Same warrant authority concept, different phase of the contract's life.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: DCMA vs. DCAA — one line each.
recall_basic.a: DCMA administers contracts and verifies systems; DCAA audits contractor cost/pricing data and rates.
d: DCMA audits rates; DCAA administers contracts.
DCMA runs the schedules program; DCAA certifies funds.
DCMA is DoD's legal support; DCAA audits for GSA.
recall_basic.x: DCMA administers contracts and verifies contractor systems; DCAA audits cost/pricing data and rates. Administration vs. audit — you'll call one for surveillance and the other for numbers.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: A contractor says "the COR told us to add it." Your flag?
recall_basic.a: Stop and check authority — all contractual direction flows through the CO.
d: No flag — CORs direct technical work.
Bill it as a constructive change and move on.
Ask the COR to confirm it in writing, then proceed.
recall_basic.x: 'The COR told us to' is the classic authority flag — stop and check before more money moves. CORs surveil; they don't direct new work. Even written COR direction doesn't cure the authority gap; it documents it.

recall_basic.q: Express vs. implied authority — the practical difference?
recall_basic.a: Express is written (the warrant); implied reasonably flows from it — both are valid.
d: Express binds the Government; implied never does.
Express is the CO's; implied is the COR's.
Implied requires ratification before it binds.
recall_basic.x: Express authority is the written warrant; implied authority reasonably flows from it (what a CO must do to execute the warrant). Both bind. The invalid lookalike is apparent authority — seeming authorized without being so.

recall_basic.q: An unlimited warrant removes what?
recall_basic.a: The dollar ceiling on the CO's authority.
d: The requirement for legal review.
The clearance gates above the SAT.
The need for a written SF 1402.
recall_basic.x: An unlimited warrant removes the dollar ceiling — nothing else. Legal review, clearance gates, and the written SF 1402 all still apply. That's why unlimited warrants demand deep experience: same rules, no financial guardrail.

recall_basic.q: Two up-front practices that prevent unauthorized commitments?
recall_basic.a: A kickoff meeting, and a letter to the contractor naming who can give direction.
d: A larger GPC program and delegated ordering.
Monthly IG inspections and CO rotations.
Withholding invoices until direction is verified.
recall_basic.x: Prevention is structural: a kickoff meeting that sets expectations, and a letter telling the contractor exactly who can give direction. UACs are trained away, not punished away — repeated ones signal a unit training gap.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: Rank the rule stack, top to bottom.
recall_basic.a: Statute → RFO → R-DFARS & deviations → DAF policy → local guidance.
d: RFO → statute → DAF policy → R-DFARS → local guidance.
Local guidance → DAF policy → R-DFARS → RFO → statute.
Statute → DAF policy → RFO → R-DFARS → local guidance.
recall_basic.x: Statute beats regulation, the RFO governs government-wide, the R-DFARS supplements for DoD, DAF policy layers under that, and local guidance sits at the bottom. Each layer adds to — never contradicts — the one above.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: What executive order launched the RFO, and when?
d: E.O. 13876, October 2024.
recall_basic.x: E.O. 14275, 'Restoring Common Sense to Federal Procurement,' April 2025 — the order behind the largest acquisition-rules rewrite in 40 years. E.O. 14402 is the other one you'll meet: contract-type justifications.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: The DAF's authoritative day-to-day contracting resource — and its catch?
recall_basic.a: The DAF Contracting Compass — it's CAC-restricted.
d: DAU's Adaptive Acquisition Framework — subscription only.
The legacy DAFFARS — being retired.
Acquisition.gov — its DoD content is restricted.
recall_basic.x: The DAF Contracting Compass is the authoritative day-to-day DAF resource — and it's CAC-restricted, which is why public guides can't reproduce it. Public DAFIs (63-138, 63-101/20-101) cover services and lifecycle policy.

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: Which appropriation buys day-to-day operations and most services — and its life?
d: RDT&E (3600) — 1 year.
O&M (3400) — 2 years.
Procurement (3010) — 1 year.
recall_basic.x: O&M (3400) buys day-to-day operations, sustainment, and most services — and lives one year for new obligations. RDT&E gets two, procurement three. Matching the need to the color is the Purpose half of the test.

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: Severable vs. non-severable services in one line.
recall_basic.a: Severable benefits as it's performed (fund ≤12 months); non-severable delivers one end product (fully fund up front).
d: Severable means under the SAT; non-severable means over it.
Severable delivers an end product; non-severable benefits as performed.
Severable is incrementally funded R&D; non-severable is O&M services.
recall_basic.x: Severable services benefit as performed (grounds maintenance) — annual money, ≤12 months, may cross fiscal years. Non-severable delivers one product (a study, an overhaul) — a bona fide need of the award year, fully funded up front.
recall_basic.ref: Field Guide Vol. 1 §5 · GAO Red Book

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: An Anti-Deficiency Act violation is what kind of problem?
recall_basic.a: Obligating more than (or before) funds are available — serious and reportable.
d: A bookkeeping error FM corrects at year-end.
A contractor overbilling issue for DCAA.
Using the wrong CLIN structure on an award.
recall_basic.x: The ADA line is Amount: obligating more than, or before, funds are available. Violations are serious, reportable, and career-relevant — it's the one fiscal statute with names attached to reports. When close to the line, FM and JA first.

recall_basic.q: Order the seven phases of the acquisition lifecycle.
recall_basic.a: Requirement → planning → solicit → evaluate → award → administer → close-out.
d: Planning → requirement → evaluate → solicit → award → administer → close-out.
Requirement → solicit → planning → award → evaluate → administer → close-out.
Market research → award → solicit → evaluate → administer → requirement → close-out.
recall_basic.x: Requirement → planning → solicit → evaluate → award → administer → close-out. The arc is the same at $9K or $90M; only the depth changes. Know the arc and every detail has somewhere to attach.

recall_basic.q: A requirement just landed on your desk. The playbook's first step?
recall_basic.a: Understand the need — what, how much, by when, for whom — and push for an IGCE.
d: Pick the contract type first.
Post a synopsis to gauge industry interest.
Confirm the money before defining the need.
recall_basic.x: Step one is always the need: what, how much, by when, for whom — pressure-tested, with an IGCE. Money, market, and method all come after, because they all depend on what's actually being bought.

recall_basic.q: The customer hands you a conclusion ("only this vendor works"). The trap?
recall_basic.a: Typing it up instead of testing it — your job is to run the steps, not ratify the answer.
d: Slowing the buy — customer conclusions are usually right.
Escalating to the HCA before doing anything.
Rejecting the requirement until it's re-scoped.
recall_basic.x: Customers hand you conclusions — 'only this vendor,' 'use it before it expires,' 'add it to the contract.' The job is testing the conclusion through the steps, not typing it. The seven-step loop IS the fast way; unwinding a bad award is the slow one.

recall_basic.q: SOW vs. PWS vs. SOO — the one-line difference.
recall_basic.a: SOW prescribes tasks; PWS defines outcomes; SOO states objectives for offerors to build on.
d: SOW is for services; PWS for products; SOO for R&D.
SOW states objectives; PWS prescribes tasks; SOO defines outcomes.
They're interchangeable labels for the same document.
recall_basic.x: SOW prescribes the tasks, PWS defines measurable outcomes, SOO states objectives and lets offerors propose the approach. The further right you go, the more competition happens on HOW — and the more the winner's proposal becomes the yardstick.

recall_basic.q: A brand-name requirement needs what?
recall_basic.a: Justification — and often a quick sources-sought reveals real competition.
d: Nothing — brand preference is the customer's call.
HCA approval at any dollar value.
A commercial item determination first.
recall_basic.x: A brand name is a competition restriction wearing a part number — it needs justification. The cheap counter is a quick sources-sought: equivalent products surface, and a risky sole source becomes a clean competition.

recall_basic.q: Match the depth of market research to what two things?
recall_basic.a: The dollar value and the complexity of the buy.
d: Schedule pressure and customer rank.
The NAICS code and set-aside status.
Funding color and fiscal-year timing.
recall_basic.x: Research depth scales with dollars and complexity — a $9K tool takes a catalog check, a $9M system takes sources-sought, industry days, and prior-buy analysis. The documented match between depth and stakes is what reviewers look for.

recall_basic.q: The three CICA buckets.
recall_basic.a: Full & open · full & open after exclusion of sources · other than full & open.
d: Sealed bid · negotiated · simplified.
Full & open · set-aside · sole source.
Competitive · urgent · directed.
recall_basic.x: Full and open; full and open after exclusion of sources (the set-aside lane — still competition); and other than full and open (the seven-exception, J&A lane). Three buckets, escalating justification burden.

recall_basic.q: A wrong exception or thin documentation in a J&A exposes you to what?
recall_basic.a: Protest exposure — the J&A must stand on documented market research.
d: Nothing, once the approving official signs.
An Anti-Deficiency Act violation.
Automatic referral to GAO.
recall_basic.x: A J&A on the wrong exception — or on thin research — is protest exposure, and approval signatures don't cure it. The J&A's strength is its evidence; GAO reads the record, not the rank of the signer.

recall_basic.q: Why does the Government insist on competition?
recall_basic.a: Better prices and quality, a broader industrial base, and process integrity.
d: Because protests are cheaper than J&As.
Mostly to develop small businesses.
To spread workload among buying offices.
recall_basic.x: Competition drives prices down, quality up, broadens the industrial base, and protects process integrity — that's why it's the statutory default, not an efficiency preference. 'We've always used this vendor' is a habit, not an exception.

recall_basic.q: What's a split purchase?
recall_basic.a: Breaking one known requirement into smaller buys to stay under a threshold — a violation.
d: Funding one buy from two appropriations.
Awarding to two vendors to build capacity.
Phasing deliveries across fiscal years.
recall_basic.x: A split purchase breaks one known requirement into pieces to duck a threshold — two $9K swipes for one $18K need. It's a violation at any tier, and the GPC program's most common finding. One requirement, one action.

recall_basic.q: What's a CLIN?
recall_basic.a: A contract line item — a discrete thing bought, with its own description, quantity, price, and funding.
d: The clause list incorporated by reference.
A contractor's labor-category identifier.
The funding document number from FM.
recall_basic.x: CLINs are the contract's skeleton: each discrete item with its own description, quantity, price, and funding. Pricing, invoicing, funding, and mods all hang off the CLIN structure — clean CLINs now save pain at every later phase.

recall_basic.q: The item is commercial — which part's streamlined terms can ride along at most dollar levels?
recall_basic.a: RFO Part 12 commercial procedures.
d: RFO Part 15 negotiation rules.
RFO Part 6 competition exceptions.
RFO Part 49 termination clauses.
recall_basic.x: Commerciality is cross-cutting: RFO Part 12's streamlined terms ride along at most dollar levels — simpler clauses, FFP preference, market pricing. Determining it early is one of the highest-leverage moves in the whole strategy.

recall_basic.q: The two contract-type families?
recall_basic.a: Fixed-price and cost-reimbursement.
d: Commercial and non-commercial.
Competitive and sole-source.
Severable and non-severable.
recall_basic.x: Fixed-price and cost-reimbursement are the two families; everything else is a variation on where risk sits between them. Learn the families and the risk bar before the six-acronym zoo — position is the load-bearing idea.

recall_basic.q: T&M contracts require what two safeguards?
recall_basic.a: A D&F that no other type works, and a not-to-exceed ceiling with active surveillance.
d: A J&A and a DCAA pre-award audit.
HCA approval and monthly invoicing.
An award-fee plan and a QASP.
recall_basic.x: T&M pays hourly rates plus materials — little incentive to control cost. So it takes a D&F that nothing else works, a hard not-to-exceed ceiling, and active surveillance. 'Flexible' for the contractor means open-ended for you.

recall_basic.q: FP-EPA exists for what situation?
recall_basic.a: Long performance periods where a fixed price needs adjustment against a named economic index.
d: R&D too uncertain to price at all.
Foreign military sales only.
Contracts paid in foreign currency.
recall_basic.x: FP-EPA holds a fixed price but adjusts against a named economic index — for long periods where locking a price would just buy inflation padding. It keeps FFP discipline while acknowledging markets move.

recall_basic.q: Price analysis vs. cost analysis in one line.
recall_basic.a: Price analysis looks at the bottom line; cost analysis digs into each element (labor, materials, overhead, fee).
d: Price analysis is for sole source; cost analysis for competition.
Price analysis applies pre-award; cost analysis post-award.
Price analysis is DCAA's job; cost analysis is the CO's.
recall_basic.x: Price analysis judges the bottom line (compare offers, history, catalogs, the IGCE); cost analysis opens the hood on each element — labor, materials, overhead, fee. Competition usually buys you out of cost analysis; sole source usually buys you into it.

recall_basic.q: Reasonableness vs. realism?
recall_basic.a: Reasonableness asks "is it too high?"; realism asks "is it unrealistically low?" (mainly competitive cost-type work).
d: Reasonableness asks "too low?"; realism asks "too high?"
They test the same thing at different dollar thresholds.
Reasonableness is subjective; realism is set by the IGCE.
recall_basic.x: Reasonableness asks 'too high?' — always. Realism asks 'unrealistically low?' — mainly on competitive cost-type work, where a lowball estimate becomes the Government's overrun. Same proposal, two different worries.

recall_basic.q: Best evidence of a fair price when competition exists?
recall_basic.a: The competing offers themselves — comparison of proposed prices.
d: The IGCE, which outranks market signals.
Certified cost or pricing data.
Last year's contract price plus inflation.
recall_basic.x: Adequate price competition is the best evidence there is — competing offers discipline each other. The IGCE is your yardstick, not a trump card; certified data is what you demand when competition CAN'T establish the price.

recall_basic.q: LPTA vs. tradeoff — when does each fit?
recall_basic.a: LPTA when "acceptable" is easy to define and risk is low; tradeoff when paying more for a better solution can be worth it.
d: LPTA above the SAT; tradeoff below it.
LPTA for services; tradeoff for supplies.
Tradeoff when schedule is tight; LPTA otherwise.
recall_basic.x: LPTA: pass/fail acceptability, award to cheapest — best when risk is low and 'acceptable' is easy to define. Tradeoff: pay more when a superior offer earns it — for less definitive requirements. The continuum is a risk dial, not a preference.

recall_basic.q: What must trace perfectly in the solicitation, or a protester will find it?
recall_basic.a: Sections L and M — what you ask for must line up with what you evaluate.
d: The IGCE and the funded amount.
The PWS and the CDRLs.
The synopsis and the award notice.
recall_basic.x: L (how to submit) and M (how you'll evaluate) must trace one-to-one. Ask for what you don't evaluate — or evaluate what you never asked for — and you've authored the protest ground yourself.

recall_basic.q: A timely, complete debrief mostly does what?
recall_basic.a: Prevents protests — it shows the process was fair. Treat it as risk management.
d: Starts the claims clock.
Waives the protester's stay rights.
Satisfies the J&A posting requirement.
recall_basic.x: A timely, complete debrief shows the process was fair — and it's the single best protest prevention there is. Treat it as risk management: an offeror who understands the decision rarely pays counsel to fight it.

recall_basic.q: The default rule on gifts from contractors?
recall_basic.a: Don't accept — the exceptions are narrow; when in doubt, decline and ask.
d: Under $50 is always fine.
Acceptable once per year, per vendor.
Fine if disclosed on your financial-disclosure form.
recall_basic.x: The default is don't accept — the exceptions are narrow and counter-intuitive, which is exactly why 'common sense' fails here. Decline, then ask the ethics counselor; a 5-minute call beats an IG referral.

recall_basic.q: Talking to a contractor about a job while working their action?
recall_basic.a: A serious conflict — disclose and recuse before going further.
d: Fine, as long as the job talk stays informal.
Allowed once you're past the competitive range.
A problem only for warranted COs.
recall_basic.x: Job-seeking while working their action is the revolving-door conflict: disclose and recuse, in that order, before anything else happens. The conflict exists at the CONVERSATION, not at the job offer.

recall_basic.q: A proposal was accidentally cc'd to a competitor. First moves?
recall_basic.a: Stop, preserve the evidence, forward nothing, and call your JA and CO today.
d: Delete it everywhere and note the incident in the file.
Ask the competitor to certify deletion, then continue.
Re-open the solicitation to level the field.
recall_basic.x: Stop, preserve, forward nothing, call JA and CO today. A mis-addressed proposal is a potential PIA disclosure — recoverable if handled loudly and fast, catastrophic if handled quietly. Deleting the evidence converts a mistake into a cover-up.

recall_basic.q: The MPT-to-SAT band carries what automatic posture?
recall_basic.a: Reserved for small business when the Rule of Two is met.
d: Reserved for 8(a) firms first.
Full and open with a small-business preference.
GPC-only, regardless of vendor size.
recall_basic.x: The MPT-to-SAT band ($15K–$350K) is automatically reserved for small business when the Rule of Two is met — the reservation comes from the dollar band itself, not from choosing SAP procedures.

recall_basic.q: Wrong NAICS code — what breaks?
recall_basic.a: The size standard, and with it the whole set-aside analysis.
d: The funding cite from FM.
The synopsis posting requirements.
Nothing — NAICS is statistical only.
recall_basic.x: The NAICS code sets the size standard — who counts as small for THIS buy. Wrong code, wrong universe, wrong set-aside call, and a size protest later. It's a decision worth five careful minutes, not a default field.

recall_basic.q: Who reviews actions for small-business opportunity?
recall_basic.a: The Small Business Professional, coordinating with the SBA.
d: The Competition Advocate.
The COCO.
The SSA.
recall_basic.x: The Small Business Professional reviews actions for small-business opportunity and coordinates with the SBA — your partner on set-aside analysis, DD 2579 coordination, and program questions. The Competition Advocate guards competition; different job.

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: The scope question in one sentence.
recall_basic.a: Would the original competitors have reasonably anticipated this change at award?
d: Is the change under 10% of contract value?
Does the contractor agree to the change bilaterally?
Is there money on the CLIN to cover it?
recall_basic.x: The scope question in one line: would the original competitors have reasonably anticipated this change at award? Anticipated → modify. Not → new work: compete it or justify it. Percentages and signatures don't answer it; anticipation does.

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: Before exercising an option, confirm what basics?
recall_basic.a: Price still fair, funds available, need still real, contractor not excluded, performance satisfactory — with timely written notice.
d: A new IGCE, a new synopsis, and fresh competition.
Just funds — the rest was settled at award.
HCA approval and an updated J&A.
recall_basic.x: Before exercising: price still fair (fresh look), funds available, need still real, contractor not excluded, performance satisfactory — plus timely written notice. The option was evaluated at award; the GATES are about now.

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: REA vs. claim — the certification difference?
recall_basic.a: The DoD REA certification applies above the SAT; the CDA claim certification above $100K — different certifications, different thresholds.
d: Same certification, two names.
Claims certify above the SAT; REAs above $100K.
Only claims ever require certification.
recall_basic.x: Two different certifications: the DoD REA certification (above the SAT, an R-DFARS requirement) and the CDA claim certification (above $100K). Different thresholds, different content, different lanes — conflating them is the classic miss.

recall_advanced.q: Five factors in the competitive-vs-sole-source call.
recall_advanced.a: Data rights sufficiency · switching/qualification costs · industrial base capability · honest urgency · second-source economics.
d: Price history · incumbent performance · schedule float · budget stability · fee structure.
Small-business impact · protest risk · clearance level · funding color · contract type.
Requirement clarity · evaluation criteria · debrief posture · option structure · NAICS fit.
recall_advanced.x: The competitive-vs-sole-source call is an evidence question, and these five factors are the evidence: can others get the data, what does switching really cost, can the base perform, is the urgency honest, and do second-source economics close. The distractor lists are real considerations — but they're downstream execution details, not the strategy call.

recall_advanced.q: What inventory precedes a sustainment competition decision?
recall_advanced.a: Data rights, deliverables (source/build/interfaces), GFP/tooling, licenses, funding.
d: Incumbent staffing, wage rates, award-fee history, subcontractor list.
CPARS ratings, DCMA findings, open claims, warranty status.
The IGCE, the acquisition plan, the QASP, and the PWS.
recall_advanced.x: Before deciding a sustainment competition, inventory what the Government actually holds: data rights, deliverables (source/build/interfaces), GFP and tooling, licenses, funding. CPARS and incumbent staffing tell you about the incumbent — the inventory tells you whether anyone else could realistically perform.

recall_advanced.q: What can never justify a bridge?
recall_advanced.a: Lack of advance planning.
d: A sustained protest on the follow-on.
A directed change in acquisition strategy.
A regulatory change late in the cycle.
recall_advanced.x: Protests, directed strategy changes, and regulatory shifts are genuinely unforeseeable — they can justify a bridge. 'We didn't plan' never can, by rule: rewarding late starts with sole-source continuations would make poor planning a strategy.

recall_advanced.q: What factors drive competitive vs. sole-source for the follow-on?
recall_advanced.a: Data rights and technical data sufficiency · qualification/switching costs and time · industrial base capability · urgency honestly assessed · lifecycle economics of a second source. Facts on each, in the file.

recall_advanced.q: How do you find out if other sources can perform?
recall_advanced.a: Fresh sources-sought and RFIs · industry days · capability analysis against the tech data package · other services'/agencies' experience with similar builds.
d: Ask the incumbent for a teaming list · check SAM registrations · rely on last cycle's research.
FPDS awards to similar NAICS · the program's engineering judgment · the IGCE basis of estimate.
A synopsis at award · SBA's Dynamic Small Business Search · DCMA capability surveys alone.
recall_advanced.x: Finding other sources takes active outreach: fresh sources-sought and RFIs, industry days, capability analysis against the tech data package, and other services' experience. Passive moves — asking the incumbent, rereading last cycle's research — find exactly what they look for: nothing.

recall_advanced.q: And if truly no one else can?
recall_advanced.a: RFO 6.103-1, one responsible source — with the J&A at the right approval tier and market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer reading it.
d: RFO 6.103-2, urgency — with the J&A signed after award and posted within 30 days.
Skip the J&A — single-source under SAP rules applies when research shows one source.
Award a bridge to the incumbent while the requirement is re-scoped for competition.
recall_advanced.x: Truly one source → RFO 6.103-1 (one responsible source), a J&A at the right approval tier, and market research strong enough to survive hostile reading. Urgency (6.103-2) is a different exception with different proof, and SAP single-source rationale stops at the SAT.

recall_advanced.q: Three types of authority — which one binds nothing?
recall_advanced.a: Express, implied, apparent — apparent binds nothing.
d: Express, implied, apparent — implied binds nothing.
Actual, delegated, apparent — delegated binds nothing.
Express, implied, apparent — all three can bind once ratified.
recall_advanced.x: Express (the warrant) and implied (what the warrant necessarily includes) are both real authority. Apparent authority — looking authorized without being authorized — binds nothing, and no amount of contractor good faith fixes it. That's the seam every UAC crawls out of.

recall_advanced.q: All six ratification elements.
recall_advanced.a: Proper-if-CO · benefit · ratifier's actual authority · fair & reasonable price · funds then and now · Legal.
d: Good faith · benefit · CO concurrence · lowest price · funds now · command endorsement.
Proper-if-CO · urgency · apparent authority · fair price · funds now · IG notification.
Benefit · contractor fault-free · ratifier one level up · price under SAT · funds then · Legal.
recall_advanced.x: All six, every time: proper if a CO had done it, benefit received, ratifier holds actual authority, price fair and reasonable, funds available then and now, Legal concurs. The distractors swap in seductive near-elements (good faith, urgency, command endorsement) — none of which are on the list.

recall_advanced.q: Who ratifies a $500K unauthorized commitment? A $90K one?
recall_advanced.a: $500K → HCA (delegable); $90K → COCO.
d: $500K → SPE; $90K → HCA.
Both → HCA — ratification authority doesn't tier by dollars.
$500K → COCO; $90K → the CO who discovers it.
recall_advanced.x: Ratification approval tiers on the SAT: above it → HCA (delegable); at or under → COCO level. $500K is over the $350K SAT, $90K is under — the card is really testing whether you carry the SAT in your head.

recall_advanced.q: Five elements of a valid contract.
recall_advanced.a: Offer/acceptance · consideration · competency · legality · certainty of terms.
d: Offer · acceptance · funding · signature · delivery schedule.
Consideration · competition · certification · clauses · closeout.
Mutual intent · fair price · written form · warrant · performance.
recall_advanced.x: Offer and acceptance, consideration, competency, legality, certainty of terms — contract law's foundation, service-agnostic. Funding, signatures, and warrants are how the GOVERNMENT contracts lawfully, but they aren't the five common-law elements this question asks for.

recall_advanced.q: What if the Government received no benefit?
recall_advanced.a: Then it can't be ratified — a ratification requires acceptance or benefit. The contractor's remedy shifts to a claim (or quantum meruit through Legal); my job is the documented record either way.

recall_advanced.q: The person who did it refuses to write a statement.
recall_advanced.a: Document the refusal, reconstruct the facts from correspondence and witnesses, and proceed — the package needs the story, and the refusal itself goes in the record.
d: Stop the ratification — without the maker's statement the package can't move.
Refer the individual to the IG and hold the contractor's invoice until they cooperate.
Have the contractor write the narrative instead; their account substitutes for the maker's.
recall_advanced.x: A refusal to write a statement doesn't stop a ratification — document the refusal, reconstruct the facts from correspondence and witnesses, and keep moving. The package needs the story; the refusal itself becomes part of the record (and a leadership conversation).

recall_advanced.q: Is implied authority real authority?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — authority reasonably inferred from a position's duties is legally valid. Apparent authority is the trap: looking authorized isn't being authorized.
d: No — only express written authority binds the Government; everything else is apparent.
Yes, but only for actions under the micro-purchase threshold.
No — implied authority binds the employee personally, not the Government.
recall_advanced.x: Implied authority is real: what reasonably flows from a position's express authority is legally valid. The trap the question hunts is conflating implied with apparent — the lookalike that binds nothing. Say the distinction cleanly and you've answered like a CO.

recall_advanced.q: Two categories of protected information under RFO 3.104.
recall_advanced.a: Source selection information; contractor bid/proposal data.
d: Classified information; controlled unclassified information.
The IGCE; the acquisition plan.
Past-performance ratings; subcontractor pricing.
recall_advanced.x: RFO 3.104 protects exactly two classes: the Government's source selection information and contractors' bid/proposal data. CUI, PII, and CPARS live under other regimes — naming the right two shows you know which law you're operating.

recall_advanced.q: Your first two containment actions on a bad disclosure.
recall_advanced.a: Legal immediately; identify/contain — recipient deletes with signed confirmation.
d: Notify the HCA; cancel the solicitation the same day.
Interview the sender; report to the IG within 24 hours.
Recall the email; brief the source selection team at the next meeting.
recall_advanced.x: First moves on a disclosure: Legal immediately, then identify and contain — the recipient deletes with signed confirmation. Cancelling the solicitation or briefing the whole team comes later, if at all, and only as the documented decision dictates.

recall_advanced.q: Where does the decision go if the disclosure impacts the procurement?
recall_advanced.a: The HCA.
d: The SSA.
GAO.
The SPE.
recall_advanced.x: When a disclosure impacts the procurement, the decision escalates to the HCA — disqualification and cancellation are HCA-level calls, with Legal driving the analysis. The SSA runs the selection; the HCA owns the integrity decision.

recall_advanced.q: Name three prevention practices you'd brief a new source selection team.
recall_advanced.a: Two-person review before release · encryption with separate passwords · disable auto-complete · SSI cover sheets (any three).

recall_advanced.q: The recipient says she deleted it — done?
recall_advanced.a: Not on her word: signed affidavit confirming deletion of all copies, and the determination still has to be written. The record closes it, not the reply email.
d: Yes — a good-faith deletion by the recipient ends the incident.
No — the solicitation must be cancelled once SSI leaves the building.
Yes, if she wasn't an offeror employee; otherwise the HCA decides.
recall_advanced.x: A verbal 'I deleted it' closes nothing. The incident closes on paper: a signed affidavit confirming deletion of all copies, plus the CO's written determination. If it went to an offeror, you're in HCA territory instead — that's the fork that matters.

recall_advanced.q: What if it went to an actual offeror?
recall_advanced.a: That's the high-impact branch: presumptive taint of the competition. HCA decision territory — disqualification or cancellation are on the table, with Legal driving.
d: Same as any spill: recipient deletes, CO documents, competition continues.
Automatic cancellation — no discretion once an offeror holds SSI.
The offeror is disqualified by operation of law; the CO just documents it.
recall_advanced.x: Disclosure to an actual offeror is the high-impact branch: presumptive taint. The HCA decides — disqualification and cancellation are both on the table — but it's a decision, not an automatic outcome. 'Delete and drive on' understates it; 'automatic cancellation' overstates it.

recall_advanced.q: A contractor employee asks your evaluator how the ratings look — violation?
recall_advanced.a: Attempting to obtain source selection information is itself a PIA problem. Document it, report it, brief the team — silence is how small probes become disclosures.
d: Not yet — the PIA reaches disclosure, not requests; nothing to report unless something was shared.
Only if the evaluator answered; log it informally and move on.
It's a violation by the contractor only if they're in the competitive range.
recall_advanced.x: ATTEMPTING to obtain source selection information is itself a PIA problem — the statute reaches the ask, not just the leak. Document it, report it, brief the team. The 'no harm until something was shared' instinct is exactly how probes escalate into disclosures.

recall_advanced.q: The three OCI types — and which is hardest to mitigate?
recall_advanced.a: Biased ground rules (hardest) · unequal access · impaired objectivity.
d: Unequal access (hardest) · biased ground rules · impaired objectivity.
Impaired objectivity (hardest) · unequal access · biased ground rules.
Financial interest (hardest) · personal conflict · organizational bias.
recall_advanced.x: Unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — and ground rules is hardest, because once a contractor shaped the requirement, no firewall un-shapes it; exclusion is the usual outcome. Ranking the types by fixability is what boards actually probe.

recall_advanced.q: The three handling tools, in order of preference.
recall_advanced.a: Avoid · neutralize · mitigate.
d: Mitigate · neutralize · avoid.
Avoid · mitigate · waive.
Disclose · firewall · exclude.
recall_advanced.x: Avoid, neutralize, mitigate — in that order of preference. Avoidance kills the conflict, neutralization structures it away, mitigation manages what remains. 'Disclose/firewall/exclude' are tools inside the framework, not the framework.

recall_advanced.q: Who approves an OCI waiver, and is it delegable?
recall_advanced.a: HCA; non-delegable.
d: HCA; delegable one level.
SPE; non-delegable.
The PCO with Legal concurrence; delegable.
recall_advanced.x: OCI waivers belong to the HCA and are non-delegable — one of the few authorities that can't move down. If your answer to any waiver question starts below the HCA, stop and climb.

recall_advanced.q: True or false: unequal access requires showing the contractor acted on the information.
recall_advanced.a: False — the access imbalance itself is the conflict.
d: True — without use, there's no competitive harm.
True — access alone is cured by a firewall certification.
False — but only if the information was source selection information.
recall_advanced.x: False — unequal access is complete on the imbalance itself; you never have to show the contractor USED the information. Requiring proof of use would gut the protection, since use is nearly unprovable. The conflict is the access.

recall_advanced.q: Which type is hardest to mitigate and why?
recall_advanced.a: Biased ground rules — once the requirement itself is shaped, a firewall can't un-shape it. Exclusion is the usual outcome.
d: Unequal access — you can never prove what information actually moved.
Impaired objectivity — self-assessment can't be firewalled, so waiver is the only cure.
Biased ground rules — because the waiver authority sits at the SPE.
recall_advanced.x: Biased ground rules — a contractor who shaped the requirement can't be firewalled out of its own influence; the spec IS the head start. That's why exclusion is the usual outcome, and why you screen for it before solicitation, not after proposals.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor firewall says the proposal team never saw anything. Enough?
recall_advanced.a: A firewall can address unequal access going forward — it does nothing for ground rules already written. Type drives remedy.
d: Yes — a certified firewall is the standard cure for all three OCI types.
No — firewalls are never acceptable mitigation; exclusion is required.
Yes, if the firewall predates the solicitation release date.
recall_advanced.x: Type drives remedy: a firewall addresses unequal access going forward, but ground rules were written in the past — no wall reaches backward. Accepting a firewall certification without typing the conflict first is the classic OCI miss.

recall_advanced.q: Who has final say on the mitigation plan?
recall_advanced.a: The PCO. Panels and reviewers advise; the decision and the accountability are mine.
d: The HCA — the same authority that owns the waiver.
Legal — an OCI is a legal determination.
The SSA, since the conflict affects the selection.
recall_advanced.x: The PCO decides on the mitigation plan — panels, Legal, and reviewers advise, but the decision and the accountability sit with the contracting officer. (The HCA's role is the waiver, a different instrument for a different situation.)

recall_advanced.q: Recite the seven responsibility standards.
recall_advanced.a: Finances · schedule · performance · integrity · organization/experience/controls · equipment/facilities · qualified & eligible.
d: Price · schedule · quality · safety · security · staffing · certifications.
Finances · past performance · size status · facility clearance · bonding · insurance · SAM.
Capability · capacity · credit · character · compliance · continuity · citizenship.
recall_advanced.x: Finances, schedule, performance record, integrity, organization/experience/controls, equipment/facilities, and otherwise qualified & eligible. The distractor lists sound like proposal evaluation — responsibility is a different gate, about the FIRM, decided at award.

recall_advanced.q: Which two system checks precede award, and at what threshold does the second apply?
recall_advanced.a: SAM exclusions always; FAPIIS over SAT ($350K).
d: FAPIIS always; SAM exclusions over the SAT.
SAM and CPARS — both at every dollar value.
SAM exclusions over the MPT; FAPIIS over $1M.
recall_advanced.x: SAM exclusions get checked on every action, no floor; FAPIIS review kicks in over the SAT ($350K). Getting the pair backwards — or giving both a threshold — is the standard miss.

recall_advanced.q: What happens when a small business is found non-responsible?
recall_advanced.a: Referral to SBA — a CoC conclusively establishes responsibility.
d: Award to the next offeror — SBA is notified after award.
The SBA gets 15 days to comment, but the CO's finding stands.
The finding is elevated to the HCA for a final determination.
recall_advanced.x: A small business found non-responsible goes to the SBA, and a Certificate of Competency conclusively establishes responsibility — the CO's finding doesn't stand against it. Skipping the referral is a protest waiting to happen.

recall_advanced.q: Doubt about capability cuts in whose favor?
recall_advanced.a: The Government's — doubt means no.
d: The contractor's — responsibility is presumed once registered in SAM.
Neither — doubt triggers a pre-award survey to resolve it first.
The contractor's, for small businesses only.
recall_advanced.x: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. There's no presumption of responsibility from SAM registration, and while pre-award surveys can inform the call, they don't reverse the default. The burden of demonstrating responsibility sits with the offeror.

recall_advanced.q: SBA issues the CoC but you still think they'll fail. Now what?
recall_advanced.a: A CoC is conclusive as to responsibility — I award, then protect the Government with administration: a solid QASP, milestone surveillance, and early engagement at the first sign of trouble. (Appeal paths exist in a dollar band — worked with Legal and SBA, not solo.)

recall_advanced.q: Can you use responsibility to screen out a contractor you distrust?
recall_advanced.a: Only on the standards, only on facts. Distrust without documentation is how a defensible "no" becomes a sustained protest.
d: Yes — responsibility is inherently a judgment call the boards won't second-guess.
No — once an offeror is otherwise successful, responsibility can't be the basis.
Only with the HCA's concurrence and a pre-award survey.
recall_advanced.x: Responsibility screens on the seven standards and documented facts — nothing else. Distrust without documentation converts a defensible 'no' into a sustained protest, because the record (not your instinct) is what GAO reads.

recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between non-responsible and ineligible?
recall_advanced.a: Ineligible = excluded (SAM/debarment) — no award, period. Non-responsible = fails the standards for this award, on today's facts.
d: They're synonyms — both mean the offeror can't receive this award.
Non-responsible = excluded in SAM; ineligible = fails the seven standards.
Ineligible is permanent; non-responsible lasts three years.
recall_advanced.x: Ineligible = excluded (SAM/debarment): no award, full stop, any dollar value. Non-responsible = fails the standards for THIS award on today's facts — a firm can be responsible next quarter. Different tests, different durations, different remedies.

recall_advanced.q: Four questions market research must answer.
recall_advanced.a: Capable sources · commercial or not · small business capability · industry practices (also: bundling justified?).
d: Best vendor · fair price · contract type · evaluation factors.
Funding color · requirement clarity · protest risk · incumbent performance.
Sources' size status · SAM registration · CPARS history · capacity.
recall_advanced.x: The four: capable sources, commercial or not, small-business capability, and industry practices (plus whether bundling is justified). 'Best vendor and fair price' is what the COMPETITION determines — research builds the map, not the pick.

recall_advanced.q: How long is research treated as current?
recall_advanced.a: 18 months.
d: 12 months.
24 months.
One fiscal year.
recall_advanced.x: 18 months — after that, research goes stale and downstream decisions citing it inherit the staleness. On long acquisitions, refresh before the J&A or set-aside decision, not after the protest.

recall_advanced.q: Name five research methods.
recall_advanced.a: Sources sought · RFI · industry day · SME/vendor engagement · prior-buy history · catalogs (any five).

recall_advanced.q: What document downstream decisions cite — and what happens if it was never written?
recall_advanced.a: The market research report; undocumented research can't support the J&A/set-aside/CID that relies on it.
d: The acquisition plan; missing research shifts the burden to the IGCE.
The sources-sought synopsis; without it the action simply proceeds full-and-open.
The D&F; undocumented research is cured by a post-award memo.
recall_advanced.x: Downstream decisions cite the market research report — the J&A, the set-aside, the CID all lean on it. Research that was never documented can't hold that weight; a post-hoc memo is reconstruction, not research.

recall_advanced.q: Your sources-sought got one response. Sole source it?
recall_advanced.a: One response to one notice isn't market absence — it's a data point. Widen the net (direct outreach, industry channels, adjacent NAICS) before concluding only one source exists; the J&A will be judged on the effort.

recall_advanced.q: How is market research different from a competition requirement?
recall_advanced.a: Research is the evidence; competition is the decision. Research tells me whether the Rule of Two is met, whether full-and-open is realistic, whether commercial procedures fit — it doesn't replace any of them.

recall_advanced.q: The PM wrote the spec around Vendor X's product. Fix it with research?
recall_advanced.a: Backwards — research should shape the requirement, not justify it after the fact. I'd push for a performance-based restatement and use the research to show what the market can actually deliver.

recall_advanced.q: The supplies priority order, top to bottom.
recall_advanced.a: Inventory → excess → UNICOR → AbilityOne → wholesale → mandatory FSS → commercial.
d: Excess → inventory → AbilityOne → UNICOR → mandatory FSS → wholesale → commercial.
Inventory → UNICOR → excess → wholesale → AbilityOne → commercial → mandatory FSS.
AbilityOne → UNICOR → inventory → excess → mandatory FSS → wholesale → commercial.
recall_advanced.x: Inventory → excess → UNICOR → AbilityOne → wholesale → mandatory FSS → commercial. The Government checks what it already owns, then statutory programs, then schedules, then the open market. Order matters — each rung must be cleared, not skipped.

recall_advanced.q: What leads the services ladder?
recall_advanced.a: AbilityOne.
d: UNICOR (Federal Prison Industries).
Agency inventories.
Mandatory Federal Supply Schedules.
recall_advanced.x: For services, AbilityOne leads the ladder — the statutory program outranks convenience. UNICOR's mandatory position applies to supplies.

recall_advanced.q: On an FSS order, who determines the order price fair and reasonable?
recall_advanced.a: The ordering contracting officer — GSA's schedule pricing doesn't substitute.
d: GSA — schedule award established reasonableness for all orders.
No one — schedule prices are reasonable by definition.
The schedule contractor certifies it with each quote.
recall_advanced.x: The ordering CO owns the order-level fair-and-reasonable call. GSA negotiated ceiling prices across the whole government — not your quantity, configuration, or competitive moment. Comparing holder quotes and seeking discounts is the ordering CO's job, not a courtesy.

recall_advanced.q: The AbilityOne item is pricier than the commercial one. Buy commercial?
recall_advanced.a: Mandatory means mandatory — if the item is on the procurement list and meets the need, price alone doesn't unlock the open market. Work fit/availability issues through the program, on the record.

recall_advanced.q: Why isn't a schedule buy automatically fair and reasonable?
recall_advanced.a: Because GSA negotiated a ceiling across the government, not my quantity, configuration, or competitive moment. Comparing quotes among holders and asking for discounts is the ordering CO's job.

recall_advanced.q: The commercial definition in one sentence, including the mod rule.
recall_advanced.a: Sold/leased/licensed to the general public (or evolved and available in time), including minor mods that don't alter form, fit, or function.
d: Sold to any Government agency in the past 12 months, including mods under 10% of value.
Catalog-priced and NAICS-coded commercial, excluding any modified item.
Available from two or more sources at market prices, with mods approved by the CID authority.
recall_advanced.x: Commercial = sold, leased, or licensed to the general public (or evolved and available in time), including minor mods that don't alter form, fit, or function. Government sales history and catalog pricing are EVIDENCE of commerciality — the definition itself runs on the public market.

recall_advanced.q: CID: at what threshold is it written, and who approves it?
recall_advanced.a: Over SAT ($350K); one level above the CO.
d: Over $1M; the CO signs their own.
Over SAT ($350K); the HCA, non-delegable.
At every dollar value; one level above the CO.
recall_advanced.x: The CID is written over the SAT and approved one level above the CO. It's a documented determination, not a checkbox — and the one-level-up approval is the piece that separates it from ordinary file documentation.

recall_advanced.q: Streamlined commercial procedures — cite and ceiling?
recall_advanced.x: RFO 12.201-1, $9M — the streamlined commercial lane. Cite and ceiling travel together at a board; one without the other is half an answer.

recall_advanced.q: Name two things Part 12 gives you and two things it takes away.
recall_advanced.a: Gets: no certified data, streamlined terms/FFP preference. Takes: only customary market data rights; Part 49 termination machinery.
d: Gets: unlimited data rights, cost transparency. Takes: FFP preference; protest exposure.
Gets: GPC use at any value, no synopsis. Takes: small-business set-asides; options.
Gets: sealed bidding, price competition. Takes: commercial warranties; T4C rights.
recall_advanced.x: Part 12 gives: freedom from certified data, streamlined terms with an FFP preference. It takes: you get only customary market data rights, and Part 49's termination machinery is replaced by the commercial clause. Knowing BOTH sides is what makes the commerciality call honest.

recall_advanced.q: How do you price it fair and reasonable without cost data?
recall_advanced.a: Market evidence: competition first, then catalog/published prices, sales history to other customers, parametric comparisons — and I can require data other than certified where the market evidence is thin.

recall_advanced.q: The mod adds an encrypted military datalink. Still minor?
recall_advanced.a: Test it against form, fit, and function of the base item — a modification that changes what the item fundamentally is or does takes you out of "minor." That's a facts-and-engineering call, documented in the CID.

recall_advanced.q: Termination for cause vs. T4D?
recall_advanced.a: Commercial contracts use the commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — Part 49's default machinery (cure notices per 49.x, excess reprocurement) doesn't apply as such. Chain warning: boards love this seam.

recall_advanced.q: The three SAP lanes and their dollar boundaries.
recall_advanced.a: GPC ≤$15K · POs $15K–$350K · BPAs for repetitive needs.
d: GPC ≤$25K · POs to $500K · BPAs above that.
GPC ≤$10K · BPAs $10K–$350K · POs above the SAT.
GPC ≤$15K · POs to $250K · IDIQs for repetitive needs.
recall_advanced.x: GPC to $15K, purchase orders from $15K to the $350K SAT, BPAs for repetitive needs (an account, not a contract). The lanes are dollar-band-driven — mixing up the boundaries collapses the whole SAP structure.

recall_advanced.q: Who is the MPT-to-SAT band reserved for?
recall_advanced.a: Small business, unless capable small sources can't be found.
d: AbilityOne and UNICOR, in priority order.
8(a) firms first, then all small business.
Local businesses within the installation's commuting area.
recall_advanced.x: The MPT-to-SAT band is reserved for small business — unless capable small sources genuinely can't be found. The reservation comes from the dollar band, and the exception requires the documented absence, not just preference for a familiar vendor.

recall_advanced.q: What documentation does an under-SAT sole source need?
recall_advanced.a: A documented single-source rationale + price reasonableness — no formal J&A.
d: A formal J&A approved by the Competition Advocate.
A D&F signed one level above the CO.
Nothing — under the SAT, source choice is unrestricted.
recall_advanced.x: Under the SAT, a sole source needs a documented single-source rationale plus price reasonableness — the formal J&A machinery lives above the SAT. 'No formal J&A' never means 'no documentation'; the file still has to carry the decision.

recall_advanced.q: Commercial streamlined ceiling and cite?
recall_advanced.x: $9M, RFO 12.201-1 — the streamlined commercial ceiling. It's the number that lets commercial buys keep SAP-like speed well past the SAT, and boards like pairing it against the $350K reflex.

recall_advanced.q: Why not spread the tool-crib buy across three GPC swipes?
recall_advanced.a: That's splitting a known requirement to evade the MPT — a bright-line violation. One $210K requirement is one purchase-order action with small business first.
d: It's allowed if each swipe stays under the cardholder's single-purchase limit.
It's fine when the shops are separate cost centers with separate funding.
GPC splits are only a violation above the SAT.
recall_advanced.x: One known $210K requirement split across GPC swipes is threshold evasion — a bright-line violation regardless of cardholder limits or cost centers. The requirement's size is measured when it's KNOWN, and it points to one purchase order with small business first.

recall_advanced.q: BPA vs. IDIQ — when does the small path stop fitting?
recall_advanced.a: A BPA is an account, not a contract — no obligation until a call. When needs get big, defined, and multi-year, the structure (and the money) belongs in a real vehicle.
d: A BPA obligates its ceiling at establishment — it stops fitting when funds run short.
BPAs convert to IDIQs automatically at the SAT; there's nothing to decide.
The paths are interchangeable — pick whichever the customer prefers.
recall_advanced.x: A BPA is a charge account — no obligation exists until a call is placed. When needs become big, defined, and multi-year, the structure and the funding belong in a real contract vehicle (IDIQ). Treating a BPA like a contract is how ceilings and fiscal discipline quietly evaporate.

recall_advanced.q: One quote came back on your $80K buy — award?
recall_advanced.a: I can, if I can call the price fair and reasonable — compare to history, catalogs, IGCE, and document it. Reasonableness rides on evidence, not on the count of quotes.
d: No — SAP requires at least three quotes before award.
Only after resoliciting once and notifying the competition advocate.
Yes — under the SAT, any received quote is presumed reasonable.
recall_advanced.x: One quote can support award if the price is provably fair and reasonable — history, catalogs, the IGCE, documented. Reasonableness rides on evidence, not on the count of quotes; a three-quote rule exists nowhere but in office folklore.

recall_advanced.q: State the Rule of Two precisely.
recall_advanced.a: Reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses submitting offers at fair market prices → set aside.
d: Two or more small businesses actually submit offers → set aside after receipt.
Two capable sources of any size → compete rather than sole-source.
Two or more quotes required on every buy over the MPT.
recall_advanced.x: Precision matters: REASONABLE EXPECTATION of two or more CAPABLE small businesses submitting offers at FAIR MARKET prices. It's a forecast made at strategy time from research — not a post-receipt count, and not a two-quote rule.

recall_advanced.q: Sole-source ceilings: HUBZone other? SDVOSB other? 8(a) DoD?
recall_advanced.x: HUBZone other: $5.5M. SDVOSB other: $5M. 8(a) DoD: $100M with no J&A (statutory basis). The half-million gap between HUBZone and SDVOSB 'other' caps is the deliberate confusable this card drills.

recall_advanced.q: What form documents specialist coordination?
recall_advanced.a: DD Form 2579.
d: DD Form 1547.
SF 30.
recall_advanced.x: DD Form 2579 documents small-business specialist coordination — the record that the set-aside analysis happened and who concurred. SF 1449 is the commercial award form; DD 1547 is weighted guidelines.

recall_advanced.q: Subcontracting plan thresholds?
recall_advanced.a: $900K; $2M construction.
d: $750K; $1.5M construction.
$1M; $2.5M construction.
The SAT; $1M construction.
recall_advanced.x: $900K standard, $2M construction — the thresholds where other-than-small primes owe a subcontracting plan. Small primes never owe one; the plan is how large business accounts for small-business opportunity below the prime level.

recall_advanced.q: Only one small business responds to your set-aside — now what?
recall_advanced.a: If the offer is fair-market priced, award — the Rule of Two tests the expectation, not the final count. Document what changed between research and offers.
d: Withdraw the set-aside and resolicit full-and-open.
Refer to the SBA for a certificate of competency before award.
Cancel and re-run the sources-sought — one offer defeats the set-aside.
recall_advanced.x: The Rule of Two tested your expectation — one responsive offer doesn't retroactively break it. If the price is fair-market, award, and document what changed between research and receipt. Withdrawing the set-aside because turnout disappointed is both unnecessary and protest bait.

recall_advanced.q: The requirement's been in the 8(a) program — can you compete it full-and-open now?
recall_advanced.a: Not unilaterally: once in 8(a), it stays unless SBA agrees to release it. That's the follow-on trap on 8(a) requirements.
d: Yes — each new requirement starts fresh; prior program history doesn't bind.
Yes, once the incumbent has graduated from the program.
Only the HCA can release it, with Competition Advocate concurrence.
recall_advanced.x: Once a requirement enters the 8(a) program, it stays unless SBA agrees to release it — the CO can't unilaterally take the follow-on full-and-open, and incumbent graduation doesn't undo the program's hold. It's the classic 8(a) follow-on trap.

recall_advanced.q: When does 8(a) sole source need a J&A?
recall_advanced.a: DoD: not below $100M. The program's statutory basis covers it — that's the 'authorized by statute' lane.
d: Above the SAT, like any other sole source.
Above $30M for DoD; $100M is the civilian line.
Never — 8(a) awards are exempt from J&As at every value.
recall_advanced.x: For DoD, 8(a) sole source needs no J&A below $100M — the program's statutory basis IS the competition exception ('authorized by statute'). The $30M figure is the civilian line; mixing the two is the standard miss.

recall_advanced.q: Recite the four SAMO carve-outs.
recall_advanced.a: SAP · statute · in-scope mods · orders under existing vehicles.
d: SAP · set-asides · urgent actions · commercial buys.
Statute · micro-purchases · options · GPC actions.
SAP · sole source · in-scope mods · bridge actions.
recall_advanced.x: SAMO: Simplified acquisition, Authorized by statute, in-scope Modifications, Orders under existing vehicles — the four lanes where CICA's full-and-open machinery doesn't attach in the first place. Distinct from the seven exceptions, which excuse competition where it DOES attach.

recall_advanced.q: Name all seven RFO 6.103 exceptions, in any order.
recall_advanced.a: One source · urgency · industrial mobilization/R&D · international agreement · statute · national security · public interest.
d: One source · urgency · follow-on · small business · statute · security · best value.
Sole source · emergency · mobilization · treaty · regulation · classification · agency head.
One source · urgency · logical follow-on · international agreement · statute · secrecy · economy.
recall_advanced.x: One source · urgency · industrial mobilization/R&D · international agreement · statute · national security · public interest. The distractors plant 'logical follow-on' and 'best value' — fair-opportunity and source-selection concepts that don't live in Part 6.

recall_advanced.q: Your J&A is $18M — who approves? $95M (DoD)? $160M (DoD)?
recall_advanced.a: $18M → Competition Advocate; $95M DoD → HPA/PEO (DoD line is $150M); $160M DoD → SPE.
d: $18M → CO; $95M → Competition Advocate; $160M → HPA/PEO.
$18M → Competition Advocate; $95M → SPE; $160M → USD(A&S).
