recall_advanced.x: In-scope mods ride the original competition — no synopsis, no new competition. Out-of-scope work is a new procurement: compete it or justify it under Part 6. The synopsis question is answered entirely by the scope analysis.

recall_advanced.q: Furnishing GFP changes the Government's posture how?
recall_advanced.a: The Government takes on performance obligations — late or faulty GFP is Government-caused delay.
d: It shifts all property risk to the contractor.
It has no schedule significance.
It converts the contract to cost-type.
recall_advanced.x: GFP puts the Government ON the performance path: late or defective property is Government-caused delay with equitable-adjustment exposure. You're not just lending equipment — you're accepting schedule obligations.

recall_advanced.q: Why do UCAs weaken the Government's negotiating position?
recall_advanced.a: The contractor performs while the price is open — comfort without cost pressure; leverage decays monthly.
d: They don't — the NTE ceiling protects the position.
Because clearance happens at award.
Because fee is locked at the UCA stage.
recall_advanced.x: Undefinitized performance is cost-reimbursement comfort at negotiation leverage: every month without a definitized price, actuals accumulate and your position decays. The caps and the 180-day clock are the counterweights — enforce them.

recall_advanced.q: Clearance protects against what, fundamentally?
recall_advanced.a: Committing the Government before an independent set of eyes checks strategy, price, and compliance.
d: Contractor default after award.
ADA violations at obligation.
Debrief disputes before award.
recall_advanced.x: Clearance is the independent check between 'we negotiated it' and 'the Government is bound by it' — strategy, price support, and compliance verified by someone who doesn't own the deal. It exists because self-review is no review.

recall_advanced.q: The agency-protest venue's superpower?
recall_advanced.a: Speed and self-correction — fixing your own error fastest, without GAO.
d: An automatic stay stronger than GAO's.
Binding precedent for future buys.
Recovery of proposal costs.
recall_advanced.x: The agency protest is fastest and self-correcting — your own agency fixing its own error without GAO's 100-day process. Its limits: no automatic-stay teeth like GAO, no binding judgment like COFC. Speed is the trade.

recall_advanced.q: Interest on a claim runs from when?
recall_advanced.a: When the CO receives the certified claim.
d: The date performance costs were incurred.
The CO's final decision.
The notice of appeal.
recall_advanced.x: CDA interest runs from the CO's RECEIPT of the certified claim — not from costs incurred, not from the final decision. That start date is why misclassifying a functional claim as an REA is expensive: the meter was already running.

recall_advanced.q: T4C exists because the Government reserves what?
recall_advanced.a: The right to end a contract in the Government's best interest — with the contractor made whole for work done.
d: The right to re-compete every contract annually.
A price-reduction remedy for market drops.
An offset against the contractor's future awards.
recall_advanced.x: T4C is the Government's reserved right to end a contract in its best interest — needs change, programs die — with the contractor made whole for work performed. It's the escape valve that makes long-term Government contracting possible at all.

recall_advanced.q: OTs trade away what, for agility?
recall_advanced.a: The mature protections framework of regulation-based contracting — spend that trade only when it buys something.
d: Intellectual-property rights entirely.
Access to nontraditional contractors.
Competition requirements — OTs are sole-source by design.
recall_advanced.x: OTs trade the mature protections framework — competition rules, cost principles, disputes machinery — for agility. That trade is worth making only when it buys something real: nontraditionals at the table, prototype-speed terms. Never as rule avoidance.

recall_advanced.q: A&E selection runs on what basis?
recall_advanced.a: Qualifications-based selection, then fair-price negotiation with the most qualified firm.
d: Lowest price among technically acceptable designers.
A best-value tradeoff, like any service.
Rotation among registered local firms.
recall_advanced.x: A&E runs on qualifications-based selection: rank firms on qualifications, negotiate price with the most qualified. Design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than design fee — the statute does that math for you.

scenarios.scenario: Eight months before a satellite-imagery software sustainment need begins, the PM tells you she's unhappy with the incumbent developer and "wants competition this time — put out an RFP next month." The system was built on the incumbent's commercial platform; the development contract delivered binaries and user manuals; the Government "probably has rights to something, nobody's checked." Two integrators have expressed informal interest, "assuming they can get the code."

facts.why: Desire isn't feasibility. An RFP before the rights-and-deliverables inventory is a solicitation you may have to cancel — strategy first, paper second.
The competition's real constraint: without source, build environments, and interface data, "assuming they can get the code" is doing tectonic work. What we hold decides what we can compete.
The platform rides its commercial license — a competitor needs lawful access. That's a licensing workstream inside the strategy, not a footnote.
Real market signal — formalize it with a sources-sought shaped around what the Government can actually furnish, and let their responses size the feasible competition.

scenarios.board_answer: Eight months is enough if we spend it right: first the data-rights and deliverables inventory — what we hold decides what we can compete; then a sources-sought built on what we can actually furnish; then the strategy call. If the inventory says competition isn't feasible yet, the honest plan may be a shorter incumbent bridge while we buy the deliverables that make next cycle competitive — and that gets written down as the strategy.

coach.qtype: an acquisition-strategy question — RFO Part 7 planning built on RFO Part 10 market research: competitive posture, timing, and what the file must prove.
coach.smes: the PM/requiring activity, Legal (JA), the Competition Advocate, and your pricing office.
coach.rule: Strategy precedes paper: no solicitation, bridge, or J&A before the rights-deliverables-market inventory is done — and lack of advance planning never justifies skipping it (RFO Part 6).

scenarios.ask: The PM wants the RFP on the street next month. How do you advise her, and what's your plan for the next eight months?
scenarios.script: This is an acquisition-strategy question — RFO Part 7 planning riding on RFO Part 10 market research: competitive posture and timing. Before I answer the RFP request, I'd pull in Legal, my pricing office, and the program engineers on data rights. The default is competition under CICA and RFO Part 6, and I want it too — but strategy precedes paper. First move is the inventory: what data rights, source code, interfaces, and tooling the Government actually holds, because what we hold decides what we can compete. Then a sources-sought built on what we can actually furnish. If the inventory says competition isn't feasible yet, the honest plan is a short, justified incumbent bridge while we buy the deliverables that make the next cycle competitive — written down as the strategy, with dates.

follow_ups.q: You said data rights decide what you can compete. Walk me through the rights levels for technical data.
follow_ups.h: Three levels, keyed to who paid for the development.
follow_ups.d: R-DFARS 227: development entirely with Government funds → unlimited rights — use, modify, disclose to anyone for any purpose. Mixed funding → Government Purpose Rights — internal use plus release for Government purposes (including competitive reprocurement under protections), converting to unlimited after the period. Entirely private expense → limited rights — internal use and emergency repair/overhaul only. The contractor asserts and proves restrictions through the assertion list; unasserted, unmarked data defaults toward the Government.

follow_ups.q: If you conclude only the incumbent can perform, what authority do you use — and who approves it?
follow_ups.h: One of the seven, plus a ladder that runs on dollars.
follow_ups.d: RFO 6.103-1, only one responsible source — a J&A built on market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer. Approval rides the RFO 6.104 ladder: the CO's certification to $900K, Competition Advocate to $20M, HPA/PEO to $90M ($150M DoD), SPE above. Post to SAM.gov within 14 days of award. For a sustainment effort of this size, expect the Competition Advocate or higher — and expect the market-research section to carry the whole document.

follow_ups.q: And if the follow-on can't award in time — what makes a bridge contract justifiable?
follow_ups.h: The cause has to be one the Government couldn't foresee.
follow_ups.d: A bridge stands on genuinely unforeseen causes — a protest, a directed strategy change, a regulatory shift — never lack of advance planning. It takes a rigorous justification: the need, the purpose and duration of the bridge, and the concrete steps that prevent the next one, in a decision memorandum. Repeat bridges escalate to higher approval each round, which is the system making planning failures progressively more expensive.

scenarios.scenario: During a staff visit you learn the fuels flight has been getting weekly analytics reports from a small software vendor since January. The squadron commander "approved it on a trial basis" after a vendor demo; the vendor now wants a PO for $95K covering the trial "as agreed." The commander points out he's a colonel with command authority, the unit genuinely uses the reports, and "there's end-of-year money to cover it." He asks you to just issue the purchase order this week.

facts.why: Rank and command authority are not contracting authority. Only a warranted CO binds the Government — this is apparent authority, which binds nothing.

facts.fact: The unit genuinely uses the reports
facts.why: Government benefit is real — that's one ratification element satisfied, and it's why ratification (not refusal) is the likely path.
The test is funds available when the commitment was made (January) and now — and the right color/year of money for what was actually received. "There's money lying around" isn't the test.
A PO now would paper over the violation. The path is a ratification package at the right level ($95K ≤ SAT → COCO), with the commander's signed statement in it.

scenarios.board_answer: That's an unauthorized commitment — command authority isn't contracting authority. I'd stop further performance, investigate, and build the RFO 1.405 ratification package: benefit's there, so it turns on fund availability in January and a fair-and-reasonable price; at $95K my COCO can ratify. And then I'd train that unit, because prevention is the real fix.

coach.qtype: an authority question — RFO 1.602 warrant authority and the RFO 1.405 ratification lane: who can bind the Government, and what happens when someone who can't, did.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) first, your COCO/flight chief, and FM for the funds picture.
coach.rule: Only a warranted CO binds the Government (RFO 1.602). Apparent authority binds nothing — an unauthorized commitment stays unratified until an official with actual authority runs all six RFO 1.405 elements.

scenarios.ask: The commander asks you to just issue the purchase order this week. What do you tell him, and what do you actually do?
scenarios.script: This is an authority question — an unauthorized commitment, RFO 1.405 territory. My phone-a-friends are Legal first, then FM on the funds picture. The default rule: only a warranted contracting officer binds the Government — command authority isn't contracting authority, so the Government isn't bound yet. I'd stop further performance today, investigate, and build the RFO 1.405 ratification package: the work would've been proper if a CO had done it, the Government clearly benefited, so it turns on funds availability back in January and a fair-and-reasonable price. At $95K, ratification sits at my COCO's level. And then I'd train that unit — kickoff meetings and a who-can-direct letter — because prevention is the real fix.

follow_ups.q: Recite all six ratification elements for me.
follow_ups.h: Proper-if… benefit… authority… price… funds… and one more signature.
follow_ups.d: RFO 1.405: (1) the action would have been proper if a contracting officer had done it; (2) the Government accepted or benefited from the supplies or services; (3) the ratifying official has actual contractual authority; (4) the price is fair and reasonable; (5) funds were available at the time of the commitment AND remain available now; (6) Legal concurs. All six, every time — the one that most often fails is funds availability at the time of the commitment.

follow_ups.q: Who ratifies, at what dollar levels?
follow_ups.h: The SAT is the split.
follow_ups.d: Over the SAT ($350K): the HCA, delegable. At or under the SAT: the COCO level. This $95K commitment ratifies at the COCO. And note who never ratifies: the person who made the commitment, or anyone in their chain trying to paper their own problem — ratification is deliberately an independent decision.

follow_ups.q: Three types of authority — which ones bind the Government?
follow_ups.h: Two are real; one only looks real.
follow_ups.d: Express authority — written and explicit, the warrant (SF 1402) — binds. Implied authority — what reasonably flows from a position's express authority — is legally valid and binds. Apparent authority — someone acting as if authorized when they aren't — binds nothing, and a contractor cannot rely on it. The colonel's command authority is real authority over his unit and zero contracting authority; that seam is where every UAC is born.

scenarios.scenario: Your SSEB chair calls: a technical evaluator just accepted a job with one of the three offerors — starting next month. The evaluator "hasn't told the team anything," has already recused himself from this week's consensus meetings, and says his new employer "only knows the program exists, nothing else." The PM wants to press on: "he recused himself, we're good — we can't slip the award for HR paperwork."

facts.fact: Evaluator accepting employment with an offeror
facts.why: Employment contacts between an offeror and a Government official with access to protected information are the PIA's second front. Self-recusal isn't self-clearing — this goes to Legal now, with a facts review of everything he touched and when the employment contact began.
His assurance isn't the standard. The question is what he had access to while employment discussions were live — that's established by record review, not by promise.
Recusal was right — but timing governs. Recusal after discussions began doesn't cure access that already happened.
Schedule pressure never outranks integrity of the selection. An award made on a tainted record invites protest and worse.

scenarios.board_answer: Recusal was step one, not the answer. I'd get Legal in immediately, establish when the employment contact started and what protected information he accessed after that, document it, and make the written determination whether the selection is compromised — and if it reached the offeror, that's the HCA's decision on how the procurement proceeds.

coach.qtype: a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104: protected information and what its movement does to the competition.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) immediately; the HCA channel if the procurement is impacted.
coach.rule: RFO 3.104 protects two classes — source selection information and contractor bid/proposal data. Contain first, document everything; the written record closes the incident, not a reply email.

scenarios.ask: The evaluator has recused himself and says no harm was done. Is this handled? What do you do?
scenarios.script: This is a Procurement Integrity Act question — RFO 3.104. Recusal was step one, not the answer — my first calls are Legal, immediately, and then the HCA channel if the facts warrant. The rule: source selection information is protected, and the danger window opened when the employment contact started, not when he told us. I'd establish exactly when that contact began, what protected information he accessed after it, and whether anything could have reached the offeror. Everything gets documented — affidavits, an MFR, and my written determination on whether the selection is compromised. If information reached an actual offeror, that's presumptive taint and the HCA decides how this procurement proceeds. The record closes this, not his reassurance.

follow_ups.q: What exactly does RFO 3.104 protect?
follow_ups.h: Two classes — one belongs to the Government, one to the offerors.
follow_ups.d: Source selection information — proposed rankings, evaluation results, the source selection plan, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate — and contractor bid and proposal information: an offeror's proprietary pricing, costs, and proposal contents. Disclosing either, or attempting to obtain it, is a violation. The PCO is the conduit and control point for all of it.

follow_ups.q: Walk me through your response steps on a suspected violation.
follow_ups.h: Legal first — then facts, containment, and a written determination.
follow_ups.d: Notify Legal immediately; gather the facts and documents; have any recipient delete all copies and confirm with signed affidavits and NDAs; notify affected parties; get an MFR from the person who disclosed; then write the determination of whether the disclosure impacts the procurement. No impact: the record goes forward for concurrence and the procurement proceeds. Impact: it goes to the HCA, who can proceed, investigate further, cancel, or disqualify an offeror.

follow_ups.q: Where do the post-Government-employment rules bite in this scenario?
follow_ups.h: The clock started at the employment contact, not the resignation.
follow_ups.d: The moment the evaluator began employment discussions with an offeror, disqualification duties attached — recusal from anything affecting that firm and prompt disclosure. His danger window isn't when he told the team; it's everything he touched after the contact began. That's why the investigation reconstructs the contact date first, then maps what protected information he accessed after it.

scenarios.scenario: Source selection for a logistics IT modernization is two weeks from FPRs. An offeror's capture manager, at an industry event, mentions to your COCO that a rival offeror "has our staffing rates — their teaming partner processes our subcontract invoices." The rival's proposal did come in with suspiciously well-aimed pricing. The SSEB chair suggests quietly normalizing the evaluated rates "so no one's advantaged," and notes that pausing now "looks bad for the program."

facts.fact: Teaming partner processes the competitor's invoices
facts.why: Classic unequal access to non-public information — a structural pipeline to a competitor's cost data. No intent needed; the imbalance is the conflict.
Evaluators can't launder an OCI through the evaluation. The conflict is investigated and resolved on the record, not adjusted away.
An award over an unresolved, documented OCI allegation looks worse — that's a sustained protest with the remedy chosen by someone else.
Suggestive but not proof. It justifies the inquiry; the determination rests on what access actually existed.

scenarios.board_answer: That allegation is unequal access — I'd get Legal in, establish the facts of what data actually flowed, and make a written determination. If access is real, I need avoidance, neutralization, or an enforceable mitigation before this selection proceeds — and note that handling an OCI during source selection isn't 'discussions,' so I can work it without opening exchanges.

coach.qtype: an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5: the type drives the remedy.
coach.smes: Legal (JA) and your reviewing chain; the HCA owns any waiver, non-delegable.
coach.rule: Identify the type first — unequal access, impaired objectivity, biased ground rules — then avoid, neutralize, or mitigate under RFO 9.5, in that order. A firewall can't fix ground rules already written.

scenarios.ask: FPRs are two weeks out. What do you do with this allegation, and does working it blow up your schedule?
scenarios.script: This is an organizational-conflict-of-interest question — RFO 9.5, unequal access to nonpublic information. Legal comes in now; the HCA owns any waiver if it comes to that. The rule: with unequal access, the imbalance itself is the conflict — I don't need proof anyone acted on it. So I'd establish the facts of what data actually flowed through that invoice-processing relationship and make a written determination. If access is real, I need avoidance, neutralization, or an enforceable mitigation plan before this selection proceeds — and the decision on that plan is mine as the PCO. One more thing for the panel: handling an OCI during source selection isn't 'discussions,' so I can work this without opening exchanges or wrecking the FPR schedule.

follow_ups.q: Name the three OCI types — and which is hardest to mitigate.
follow_ups.h: Access, objectivity, and the one where the requirement itself is shaped.
follow_ups.d: RFO 9.5: unequal access to nonpublic information — the imbalance itself is the conflict, no bad act required; impaired objectivity — the contractor would evaluate its own work; and biased ground rules — the contractor shaped the requirement it now wants to compete on. Biased ground rules is hardest: no firewall un-writes a spec, so exclusion is the usual outcome. Impaired objectivity is the type most likely to be waived.

follow_ups.q: What are your three handling tools, in order of preference?
follow_ups.h: Kill it, structure it away, or manage it.
follow_ups.d: Avoid — exclude the source or remove the conflicted work from the requirement; neutralize — remove the contractor from the specific conflicted activity; mitigate — reduce the impact to an acceptable level through a formal, enforceable mitigation plan. In that order. If none works and the benefit still outweighs the conflict, the waiver lane exists — HCA approval, non-delegable.

follow_ups.q: Who has final say on the mitigation plan?
follow_ups.h: Panels advise. One signature decides.
follow_ups.d: The PCO. The review machinery — Legal review, the OCI panel with its recommendations — advises, but the decision and the accountability sit with the contracting officer. Say that plainly at the board: 'the panel recommends; I decide, and I own it.' It's exactly the kind of authority question panels probe to see if you know where your own signature sits.

scenarios.scenario: Award week on a grounds-maintenance IDIQ set-aside. Your apparent awardee — a small business — was terminated for default by another base fourteen months ago; their proposal explains new ownership and a rebuilt crew. The PM forwards a rumor from the old contract's COR that "these guys always bail mid-summer." Your specialist notes they're clean in SAM. The customer wants award Friday because the mowing season "won't wait for paperwork."

facts.why: A recent default squarely engages the performance-record standard. It's not automatically disqualifying — but it must be weighed on the record against the new-ownership facts.
Exactly the kind of countervailing fact the determination exists to evaluate. Verify it — org charts, key personnel, financing — don't just quote the proposal.
Hearsay isn't a finding. Chase it to documented performance history (CPARS, the T4D record) or drop it.
Necessary, not sufficient — exclusions and responsibility are different gates.
If the facts add to non-responsible, the SBA referral happens regardless of the mowing season — and the CoC may still direct award.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd make the determination on documented facts — the default record versus verified evidence of new ownership and capacity. Clean SAM isn't the test, and rumors don't count. If I land on non-responsible, they're small, so it goes to SBA for the CoC decision — and Friday moves if it has to.

coach.qtype: a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts.
coach.smes: your contracting chain, Legal, and the SBA — a small-business referral is mandatory under RFO Part 19, and a CoC is conclusive.
coach.rule: Doubt cuts in the Government's favor — doubt means no. But the 'no' must stand on the RFO 9.104 standards and documented facts, never on undocumented distrust.

scenarios.ask: Award is scheduled Friday. Can you award to this contractor — and what do you do about the rumor?
scenarios.script: This is a responsibility question — the seven RFO 9.104 standards, applied to today's facts. My help: my chain, Legal, and the SBA, because this offeror is small. The default: doubt cuts in the Government's favor — but doubt has to stand on documented facts, not rumors. So I'd verify: is the new ownership real, is the rebuilt crew under contract, what does the default record actually show against the standards for performance and integrity? Rumors from a competitor don't count and clean SAM isn't the test. If I land on non-responsible, referral to SBA is mandatory under RFO Part 19 — and a Certificate of Competency, if issued, is conclusive. Friday moves if it has to; an award I can't defend moves nothing.

follow_ups.q: Recite the seven responsibility standards.
follow_ups.h: Money, time, record, character, organization, gear, and eligibility.
follow_ups.d: RFO 9.104: adequate financial resources or the ability to obtain them; ability to comply with the delivery or performance schedule; a satisfactory performance record; a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; the necessary organization, experience, accounting and operational controls, and technical skills; the necessary equipment and facilities; and otherwise qualified and eligible under applicable laws.

follow_ups.q: What system checks precede award, and at what threshold?
follow_ups.h: One always; one over the SAT.
follow_ups.d: SAM exclusions on every action, no floor — an excluded contractor is ineligible, period. FAPIIS review for actions over the SAT ($350K) — the integrity and performance record system where things like that prior default live. This scenario is exactly why the FAPIIS check exists: it surfaces history a clean SAM search and a fresh CAGE code won't.

follow_ups.q: SBA issues the CoC — can you appeal it?
follow_ups.h: There's a dollar band where you can.
follow_ups.d: A Certificate of Competency conclusively establishes responsibility — you award. The CO may appeal a CoC for actions between $100K and $25M, worked through channels with Legal and SBA. Above $25M there's no appeal, only a request for SBA Headquarters review. And either way, the Government's protection shifts to administration: a hard QASP, milestone surveillance, early engagement at the first slip.

scenarios.scenario: A depot needs specialized corrosion-inspection services, estimated $4.5M over three years. The incumbent's contract ends in five months. The PM hands you last cycle's market research — dated 26 months ago — showing "only the incumbent responded," plus an email from the incumbent's BD lead helpfully listing why competitors "can't meet the certification requirements." Your specialist mentions two small firms recently won similar work at another command.

facts.why: Past the 18-month currency line — it can inform, but it can't carry a new strategy. Fresh research is step one.

facts.fact: Incumbent's list of why competitors can't perform
facts.why: Market intelligence authored by the party that benefits from no competition is not market research. Verify independently or discard.

facts.fact: Two small firms winning similar work elsewhere
facts.why: Live evidence of capability — chase it: scope comparability, certifications, capacity. It bears directly on the Rule of Two.
Tight but workable — and "no time to research" is how bad bridges get born. The timeline argues for starting now, not skipping it.

scenarios.board_answer: That research is stale and the most persuasive document in the file was written by the incumbent — I'd run a fresh sources-sought now, engage the two small firms directly, and let the results drive the set-aside and competition decisions. Five months is enough if we start today; if it slips, a short bridge with a real cause beats a sole source built on a competitor's brochure.

coach.qtype: a market-research question — RFO Part 10: evidence before decisions.
coach.smes: the requiring activity's SMEs, your Small Business Professional, and industry itself — sources sought, RFIs, industry days.
coach.rule: RFO Part 10 research is the evidence; the commerciality, competition, and set-aside calls are decisions built on it. Undocumented research supports nothing downstream — and RFO 10.001 treats it as current for 18 months.

scenarios.ask: The PM says the research is done and only the incumbent can perform. How do you proceed with five months left?
scenarios.script: This is a market-research question — RFO Part 10: research is the evidence under every decision that follows. My partners here are the requiring activity's engineers, my Small Business Professional, and industry itself. The rules: research goes stale at 18 months under RFO 10.001, and this file is 26 months old — worse, its most persuasive document was written by the incumbent. So I'd run a fresh sources-sought today, engage the two small firms directly, and let real results drive the set-aside and competition calls. Five months is enough if we start now. If it slips anyway, a short bridge with a genuine cause beats a sole source built on a competitor's brochure — and the J&A that research would produce wouldn't survive a protest anyway.

follow_ups.q: What questions must market research answer?
follow_ups.h: Sources, commerciality, small business, practices — and one about consolidation.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 10: are there capable sources; is the requirement commercial (or satisfiable by non-developmental items); can small businesses perform; what are the industry's customary practices and terms; and is any bundling or consolidation justified. Those answers drive the set-aside call, the commerciality determination, the competition strategy, and how the requirement itself gets defined.

follow_ups.q: How long is research current, and what document carries it?
follow_ups.h: A shelf life and a report.
follow_ups.d: Current within 18 months under RFO 10.001 — this file's 26-month-old research fails on its face. And the market research report is the document every downstream decision cites: the J&A, the set-aside determination, the CID. Research that was never documented can't support any of them — a post-hoc memo is reconstruction, not research.

follow_ups.q: Name five research methods you'd actually run here in the next two weeks.
follow_ups.h: Active outreach beats passive posting.
follow_ups.d: A properly shaped sources-sought (right NAICS, real title, adequate window); direct RFIs to the two small firms and known integrators; prior-procurement review in FPDS for who's winning similar work; SME and vendor engagement — actual conversations, documented; and a compressed industry day or one-on-ones if responses warrant. Depth scales to the dollar value: $4.5M with a sole-source question hanging on it deserves all five.

scenarios.scenario: A squadron wants 400 task chairs "identical to the ones facilities bought last year from a local dealer — we already have a quote." Your inventory manager mentions a warehouse annex holding surplus furniture from a recently consolidated unit. The dealer's quote is 8% below the GSA schedule price for a comparable chair, and the squadron notes AbilityOne "only makes the fabric panels, not the chairs."

facts.why: Agency inventory and excess sit at the top of the ladder — before anyone's quote matters, that annex gets checked and the result documented.
Attractive, but the ladder isn't priced-ordered — it's priority-ordered. The quote matters only when the buy legitimately reaches the commercial rung (and then it's useful pricing evidence).
Fine — check the procurement list for what's actually covered and document the non-fit. That's the rung working as designed.

scenarios.board_answer: Ladder first: inventory and that annex, then UNICOR and AbilityOne against the procurement list, then schedules — and only then the dealer, whose quote becomes price-comparison data, not a shortcut. The file shows each rung and why we moved past it.

coach.qtype: a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder before the open market.
coach.smes: your policy shop, the AbilityOne/UNICOR program channels, and the schedule's ordering guide.
coach.rule: Work the RFO Part 8 ladder in order — inventory, excess, UNICOR, AbilityOne, schedules — and mandatory means mandatory; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.

scenarios.ask: The squadron has a quote in hand and wants the chairs ordered this week. What's your buying path?
scenarios.script: This is a required-sources question — the RFO Part 8 priority ladder comes before the open market. My help: the inventory manager, the AbilityOne procurement list, and our policy shop. The rule: the ladder is mandatory and runs in order — Government inventory and that surplus annex first, then UNICOR and AbilityOne against the procurement list, then schedules, and only then commercial. The dealer's quote doesn't jump the line; it becomes price-comparison data when and if we lawfully reach the open market. The file shows each rung and why we moved past it — that documentation is what makes the eventual buy defensible, whatever rung it lands on.

follow_ups.q: Recite the supplies priority ladder, top to bottom.
follow_ups.h: What the Government owns, then statute, then schedules, then market.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 8: (1) existing Government inventory; (2) excess property from other agencies; (3) Federal Prison Industries — UNICOR; (4) AbilityOne procurement-list items; (5) wholesale supply sources; (6) mandatory Federal Supply Schedules; (7) commercial sources. In order, each rung checked and documented before moving past it.

follow_ups.q: How does the ladder change for services?
follow_ups.h: The statutory program leads.
follow_ups.d: For services: AbilityOne first, then Federal Supply Schedules, then Federal Prison Industries, then commercial sources. Shorter ladder, same discipline — and the same rule that being on the AbilityOne procurement list makes the source mandatory, with price alone never unlocking the open market.

follow_ups.q: If this lands on a schedule buy — who determines the order price fair and reasonable?
follow_ups.h: GSA priced the schedule. Who prices the order?
follow_ups.d: The ordering contracting officer. GSA's determination established schedule-level ceiling prices — not your quantity, your configuration, or your competitive moment. Compare quotes among schedule holders carrying the item, seek discounts (schedule prices are ceilings), and document the comparison as your price analysis. That documentation is the difference between an order and a defensible order.

scenarios.scenario: A prime's $22M avionics upgrade proposal includes an $8M subsystem the prime bought "commercially" from its own subsidiary. Support: a one-page assertion citing "regular commercial sales," a catalog page with no prices, and a note that "per Part 12, no cost data is required." The subsidiary has sold the subsystem to exactly two customers — both foreign militaries — and your engineer says the Government's configuration adds a hardened chassis and MIL-STD wiring.

facts.why: "Sold to the general public" is the definition's spine — military-only sales history undercuts the assertion at its root. This is the fact to chase first.
Modifications get tested against form/fit/function. Militarization of this scale strains "minor."
A catalog proves a brochure exists. Commerciality pricing runs on actual sales at market prices — demand the sales data.

facts.fact: Prime bought from its own subsidiary
facts.why: An affiliated "commercial sale" deserves double scrutiny — the arms-length pricing discipline isn't there.
Backwards — the exception applies only after the determination holds. Assertion isn't determination.

scenarios.board_answer: The Government makes the commerciality call, not the proposal. On these facts — military-only sales, an affiliated seller, and militarizing mods — I'd likely find it non-commercial; and even if some element qualifies, I still require data sufficient to price it, certified or otherwise. The one-page assertion gets returned with a data demand attached.

coach.qtype: a commerciality question — the RFO 2.101 definition, the CID, and what RFO Part 12 changes.
coach.smes: your pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above you.
coach.rule: Commercial rides the market: the RFO 2.101 definition (including minor mods that keep form, fit, and function) is a documented CID call over the SAT, and RFO Part 12 trades certified data for market evidence.

scenarios.ask: The prime says no cost data is required on the $8M 'commercial' subsystem. How do you evaluate this proposal?
scenarios.script: This is a commerciality-and-pricing question — RFO 2.101 and Part 12. My help: my pricing office, Legal, and the CID approval level one above me. The rule: the Government makes the commerciality determination — a proposal can assert it, but it can't declare it. On these facts — military-only sales, an affiliated seller, militarizing modifications — the assertion likely fails: that's not 'sold to the general public,' and the mods look like they change form, fit, or function. And here's the key move: even if some element qualifies as commercial, that excepts certified data, not data — I still require information sufficient to find the price fair and reasonable. The one-page assertion goes back with a data demand attached.

follow_ups.q: Recite the commercial-item definition for me.
follow_ups.h: Who it's sold to, plus the evolution and minor-mod branches.
follow_ups.d: RFO 2.101: an item sold, leased, or licensed to the general public — or evolved from such an item and available in time to meet the Government's need — including minor modifications that don't alter the item's form, fit, or function. For services: installation, maintenance, repair, or training for commercial products, or services sold competitively at catalog or market prices. The general-public element is what one foreign military sale and an affiliate transaction both fail.

follow_ups.q: What does the written CID require, and who approves it?
follow_ups.h: Over the SAT, one level up, with a comparison behind it.
follow_ups.d: For DoD actions over the SAT ($350K): a written Commercial Item Determination approved one level above the contracting officer — describing the item, stating the basis for meeting the definition with a comparison analysis, signed and dated. Relying on a prior CID requires addressing how current market conditions affect the earlier finding. The determination is the Government's call, made on evidence the vendor supplies.

follow_ups.q: Say it holds up as commercial — what pricing data can you still demand?
follow_ups.h: The exception excepts the certificate, not the data.
follow_ups.d: Data other than certified cost or pricing data, sufficient to determine the price fair and reasonable: sales history to other customers, catalog and market prices, quantity-discount structures, and supporting quotes. Commerciality removes the certification requirement and the defective-pricing remedy — it never removes the CO's duty to price the action on evidence. No data, no deal applies to commercial buys too.

scenarios.scenario: Friday, end of September. The CE squadron brings you four "urgent" buys: $14,800 of hand tools (GPC-ready, they say), another $14,600 of the same catalog's power tools, a $95K generator "only Vendor Z sells with the right output curve," and a request to "set up something so we stop doing paperwork every month" for HVAC filters. The GPC holder mentions the two tool buys "are from the same order the shop chief wrote up — we just split it to keep it simple."

facts.why: Same requirement, same catalog, same write-up: that's a ~$29K buy split to stay under the $15K MPT — the textbook violation. Recombine it into a purchase order, small business first.
Under-SAT sole source: document the single-source rationale (the output-curve requirement) and the price reasonableness — no J&A, but the reasoning goes on paper.
Repetitive, predictable, small: a BPA with established sources is the designed answer.
Fiscal-year pressure doesn't change any lane's rules — it's why the lanes exist. Fast is fine; splitting isn't.

scenarios.board_answer: The tool buys are one requirement — recombining them puts it in the purchase-order lane, reserved for small business. The generator is a documented under-SAT sole source. The filters become a BPA. And September doesn't amend Part 13.

coach.qtype: a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13: the right lane by dollar band.
coach.smes: your GPC program coordinator, Small Business Professional, and COCO.
coach.rule: The band picks the RFO Part 13 lane: GPC to $15K, purchase orders to the $350K SAT — reserved for small business under the RFO Part 19 Rule of Two — and splitting a known requirement to stay under a threshold is a bright-line violation.

scenarios.ask: It's the last week of September and the squadron wants all four buys executed now. What's lawful, what isn't, and what's your plan?
scenarios.script: This is a simplified-acquisition question — RFO Part 13 — with a fiscal-year costume on. My help: the GPC coordinator, my Small Business Professional, and FM. The rules: splitting one known requirement to stay under the micro-purchase threshold is a bright-line violation — the tool buys are one requirement, so recombined they're a purchase-order action in the small-business-reserved band. The generator can be an under-SAT sole source with a documented single-source rationale and price-reasonableness support — no J&A needed, but documentation absolutely. The recurring filters belong on a BPA. And I'd say it plainly: September doesn't amend Part 13 — expiring money never converts a violation into a technique.

follow_ups.q: What are the three SAP buying methods, and their dollar boundaries?
follow_ups.h: A card, an order, and an account.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 13: the Government Purchase Card for micro-purchases at or under $15K; purchase orders from $15K up to the $350K SAT — a Government order the contractor accepts in writing or by performance; and Blanket Purchase Agreements for repetitive needs from established sources — an account, not a contract, with no obligation until a call is placed.

follow_ups.q: What competition does SAP actually require at these values?
follow_ups.h: Reserved band, local solicitation, synopsis line.
follow_ups.d: The MPT-to-SAT band is reserved for small business under the Rule of Two. Under $25K, solicit at least three vendors; over $25K, synopsize on SAM.gov. Award can be made on price alone, but price reasonableness must always be supportable — quotes, history, catalogs, the IGCE. Streamlined never means standard-free; it means proportionate documentation.

follow_ups.q: When does an under-SAT sole source need a J&A?
follow_ups.h: It doesn't — but it needs something.
follow_ups.d: Never — the formal J&A machinery starts above the SAT. Under it, a sole source needs a documented single-source rationale (why only Vendor Z's generator meets the need) plus price-reasonableness support. That's the generator's lane here: no J&A, but real documentation. The trap is hearing 'no J&A' as 'no file' — the rationale still has to survive a reviewer.

scenarios.scenario: A $4.7M base supply-chain analytics requirement is ready to solicit. Your predecessor's file shows it was once an 8(a) award "years ago," then competed full-and-open last cycle after "SBA released it" (no release letter in the file). Research finds one very capable WOSB and one small firm whose capability statement is generic. The PM suggests a WOSB sole source "since she's clearly the best," and notes the incumbent large business "will protest anything we do anyway."

facts.why: If the requirement was never properly released from 8(a), its current posture is built on sand — confirm with SBA before any strategy is chosen. The paper matters.

facts.fact: One strong WOSB + one generic small firm
facts.why: The Rule of Two needs a reasonable expectation of two capable offerors — a generic capability statement gets probed, not presumed. The set-aside call turns on this.

facts.fact: "WOSB sole source, she's clearly the best"
facts.why: WOSB sole source has conditions and a ceiling — "best" isn't the test, and at $4.7M it must actually fit the program's sole-source lane ($5.5M other) and its conditions.
Protest fear is not a strategy input — a defensible record is the protest strategy.

scenarios.board_answer: First I'd confirm the 8(a) release with SBA — that decides whose requirement this even is. Then the Rule of Two on real capability evidence: if the second small firm doesn't hold up, a WOSB sole source is only available if the program's conditions and ceiling genuinely fit at $4.7M — otherwise compete it and let the record carry the protest.

coach.qtype: a small-business question — RFO Part 19: the Rule of Two and the program lanes.
coach.smes: your Small Business Professional and the SBA PCR; DD Form 2579 documents the coordination.
coach.rule: RFO Part 19: a reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses at fair market prices → set it aside. The rule tests the expectation at strategy time, not the final offer count.

scenarios.ask: How do you structure the competition — and does the 8(a) history change what you're allowed to do?
scenarios.script: This is a small-business-programs question — RFO Part 19, with an RFO 19.8 8(a) trap inside it. My first calls: my Small Business Professional and the SBA district office, plus Legal. The controlling rule: once a requirement enters the 8(a) program it stays there unless SBA agrees to release it — and there's no release letter in this file, so before anything else I confirm that release with SBA, because it decides whose requirement this even is. Then the Rule of Two on real capability evidence: if two capable small firms hold up at fair market prices, it's a set-aside. A WOSB sole source only enters if the program's conditions and caps genuinely fit at $4.7M. Otherwise compete it and let the documented record carry any protest.

follow_ups.q: When does an 8(a) sole source need a J&A?
follow_ups.h: There's a dollar line, and it's high for DoD.
follow_ups.d: For DoD, not below $100M ($30M for civilian agencies) — below those lines the program's statutory basis is the competition authority, the 'authorized by statute' lane, no J&A required. SBA must approve the contract. Above the lines, a J&A enters. Know the pair: $100M DoD / $30M civilian is a favorite board number.

follow_ups.q: Where does competitive 8(a) begin?
follow_ups.h: Same number family as the HUBZone and WOSB caps.
follow_ups.d: Competitive 8(a) when at least two eligible firms are expected and the value exceeds $8.5M for manufacturing or $5.5M for everything else. Below those, sole source within the program is available. The $8.5M/$5.5M pair recurs across HUBZone and WOSB sole-source caps (SDVOSB runs $8.5M/$5M) — learn it once as a family and the board can't rattle you with any of them.

follow_ups.q: One more wrinkle: what changed in the 8(a) program recently that you'd verify before relying on it?
follow_ups.h: Eligibility standards shifted in early 2026.
follow_ups.d: As of January 2026, SBA moved the program to strictly race-neutral eligibility standards following litigation — admissions dropped sharply and many participants were affected. Before building a strategy on 8(a), verify the firm's current program status with SBA and your Small Business Professional. It's also a model board answer: naming a live regulatory shift shows you're current, and 'I'd verify before relying' is always the right closing note.

scenarios.scenario: A PM bursts in: her ground-station modernization needs a new encryption module integrated "immediately — the wing commander is asking weekly." The incumbent integrator says it can start Monday. She's drafted a memo titled "Sole Source Justification — Urgent" for your signature, and adds that since the module rides on the incumbent's existing $60M integration contract, "we can probably just add it as a mod anyway." The module work is estimated at $2.8M. The existing contract's SOW covers "integration of communications and crypto subsystems as identified in the modernization baseline" — and this module is in the approved baseline.

facts.why: Pressure language pulling you toward a 6.103-2 urgency J&A. Command interest is not unusual and compelling urgency — no quantified harm, no mission stoppage.

facts.fact: The drafted "Sole Source Justification — Urgent" memo
facts.why: Someone else picked your authority before you analyzed the action. The board wants you to re-derive it.

facts.fact: SOW covers crypto subsystems in the approved baseline
facts.why: This is the fact that decides it: the work is arguably in scope of the existing contract. Run the scope analysis (Part 43 thinking: would offerors have anticipated it? cumulative impact?). If it's in scope, it's the M in SAMO — CICA doesn't apply and there is no J&A to write.
If scope analysis says it's new work, the action is over SAT → full and open unless a 6.103 exception holds, and at $2.8M your J&A approver would be the Competition Advocate.

scenarios.board_answer: Before I talk exceptions, I'd do a scope review with Legal — if this module is within the existing contract's scope, CICA doesn't govern and we execute a mod. If it's out of scope, competition is the default at $2.8M, and I'd need market research to support any 6.103-1 justification — command interest alone won't carry a 6.103-2 urgency.

coach.qtype: a competition question — CICA and RFO Part 6: the default and the exception ladder.
coach.smes: the Competition Advocate, Legal, and fresh market research to test the premise.
coach.rule: Full and open is the default over the SAT (RFO 6.101). 'Other than' takes one of the seven RFO 6.103 exceptions in a J&A approved at the RFO 6.104 tier — and 'we've always used them' is not one of the seven.

scenarios.ask: The PM has the sole-source memo drafted and the commander is asking weekly. What's your answer?
scenarios.script: This is a competition question — CICA and RFO Part 6 — but scope comes first. My help: Legal on the scope review, then the Competition Advocate if we end up in exception territory. The order of analysis matters and I'd say it in this order: first, if this encryption module is within the existing contract's scope under RFO Part 43, CICA doesn't even govern — we execute a modification and we're done. If it's out of scope, it's a new $2.8M requirement and full and open competition is the default. A 6.103-1 one-source justification needs market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer, and command interest alone won't carry 6.103-2 urgency — urgency is about mission harm, quantified, not about who's asking.

follow_ups.q: By the way — name all seven exceptions to full and open competition.
follow_ups.h: One source, urgency, mobilization… keep going to seven.
follow_ups.d: RFO 6.103: (1) only one responsible source; (2) unusual and compelling urgency; (3) industrial mobilization, or engineering/developmental/research capability; (4) international agreement; (5) authorized or required by statute — UNICOR, AbilityOne, 8(a); (6) national security; (7) public interest — extremely rare, agency-head level. Recite them cold: this is the single most-asked list at the board.

follow_ups.q: Walk me up the J&A approval ladder.
follow_ups.h: Four rungs, and the DoD line at the top differs.
follow_ups.d: RFO 6.104, at October 2025 values: to $900K, the contracting officer's certification is the approval; above $900K to $20M, the Competition Advocate; above $20M to $90M — $150M for DoD — the Head of the Procuring Activity or PEO; above that, the Senior Procurement Executive. Post the J&A to SAM.gov within 14 days of award, 30 for urgency. This $2.8M action, if it goes sole source, sits with the Competition Advocate.

follow_ups.q: And when does CICA not apply at all?
follow_ups.h: Four carve-outs — the mod lane is the one in play here.
follow_ups.d: CICA doesn't govern: simplified acquisitions under Part 13; actions under statutory authorities like the Federal Supply Schedules; in-scope modifications under Part 43; and task or delivery orders under existing IDIQs, which run on RFO 16.505 fair opportunity instead (Other Transactions also sit outside). That's why the scope review comes first in this scenario — if the module is in scope, we're in the mod lane and the whole exceptions conversation never starts.

follow_ups.q: Say urgency is real — what must the J&A quantify, and what limits ride with it?
follow_ups.h: Harm, breadth, duration, and a posting clock.
follow_ups.d: An RFO 6.103-2 urgency J&A quantifies the serious harm to the Government — mission failure, safety, unacceptable operational delay — not the commander's interest level. Limits: solicit as many sources as practicable even under urgency; duration limited to about one year; and the J&A may follow the award but must be posted within 30 days. Urgency buys speed, never silence.

scenarios.scenario: Tradeoff selection, $45M, discussions closed, FPRs in. Offeror A: slightly lower rated, price well below the Government's probable cost. Offeror B: modestly better ratings, much higher price. The SSEB chair worries B "will protest if they lose." Then you learn the SSA — without you — called Offeror A, told them their price "is way out of line with our probable cost," flagged conflicts between their EN responses and their FPR, and "gave them three ways to fix it."

facts.why: That call was discussions — after FPRs, with one offeror, inviting revision. Unequal exchanges with a single offeror after close is about as serious as Part 15 problems get. Stop everything; Legal now.

facts.fact: "Three ways to fix it" — compounds it
facts.why: Coaching one offeror toward award is disparate treatment on the record — the remedy has to be structural, not cosmetic.
Legitimately handled through the evaluation itself (realism on cost-type; risk assessment otherwise) — it never justified an off-record call.
Protest fear caused this mess. The cure is a clean record, and now likely: document the breach, reopen discussions with all offerors in the range, fresh FPRs — done with Legal's hand on the wheel.

scenarios.board_answer: My concerns are unequal discussions after close and disclosure of our probable cost to one offeror. I'd halt award, document the exchange, and with Legal likely reopen discussions with every offeror in the range and take new FPRs — the only fix for unequal treatment is restored equal treatment, on the record.

coach.qtype: a source-selection question — RFO Part 15: fair process, documented judgment.
coach.smes: the SSA, your SSEB chairs, Legal, and the pricing office for the cost/price side.
coach.rule: The solicitation is the contract of the competition: evaluate exactly as Section M promised, keep RFO Part 15 exchanges in their lanes — clarifications, communications, discussions — and make discussions meaningful.

scenarios.ask: What are your concerns with what the SSA did, and what — if anything — can fix it?
scenarios.script: This is a source-selection integrity question — RFO Part 15 exchange rules meeting RFO 3.104. My immediate help: Legal, and this conversation happens before any award moves. The rules broken: discussions after close with one offeror — unequal treatment — and disclosure of our probable cost to a competitor, which is source selection information. The fix has to restore equality, on the record: halt the award, document exactly what was said, and with Legal, likely reopen discussions with every offeror remaining in the range and take new FPRs from all of them. What I can't do is paper over it — an award on this record invites a protest we'd deserve to lose, and the PIA implications of the disclosure get their own written determination.

follow_ups.q: Define the three exchange types and the lines between them.
follow_ups.h: The competitive range is the boundary; revisions are the tell.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 15: clarifications — minor or clerical issues, no proposal revisions; communications — before the competitive range, to understand proposals well enough to set the range, still no revisions; discussions — after the range is established, with every offeror in the range, and offerors may revise. The moment an exchange invites a revision, it's discussions — with all of discussions' obligations attached.

follow_ups.q: What makes discussions 'meaningful'?
follow_ups.h: Each offeror hears its own weaknesses — with enough substance to act.
follow_ups.d: Each offeror in the range must be told its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond — tailored to that proposal, not a generic list, and even-handed across the range. What the SSA did here fails every element: one offeror, after close, fed the Government's cost position. Meaningful discussions are the protest-proofing of a source selection; unequal ones are the protest.

follow_ups.q: Who does what — SSA, SSEB, SSAC, PCO?
follow_ups.h: Decide, evaluate, compare, run the business.
follow_ups.d: The SSA is the decision-maker — appoints the boards, approves the range, can award without discussions if the solicitation allowed it; under $10M the PCO typically serves as SSA. The SSEB evaluates each proposal against Section M — individually, never comparing offerors. The SSAC (required over $100M) does the comparative analysis and recommends. The PCO runs the business side: the range determination, exchanges, award, debriefs — and protects proposal confidentiality.

topics: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
scenarios.scenario: July 2026. You're the PCO for a sole-source $14M FPIF production add-on to a fielded ground radar — a new contract action, proposal in hand. The prime's proposal includes a $6M subcontract for RF amplifier modules with a ground rule: "the subcontract is commercial — pricing detail cannot be provided." The PM notes the original radar contract "was competed three years ago, so pricing's already been scrubbed," and finance wants award before the fiscal year closes. The prime's cover letter offers "summary-level cost data in the interest of schedule."

facts.why: Post-cutover action over $10M, sole source, no exception on its face → certified cost or pricing data is required. "Summary-level in the interest of schedule" doesn't satisfy the statute.
Adequate price competition excepts the action that was competed. This action wasn't. The exception fails at the action level.

A commercial determination, if it holds, excepts the subcontract from certified data — it does not excuse the prime's obligation, and I still need data other than certified sufficient to find the subcontract price fair and reasonable. First question: does the commercial assertion actually survive scrutiny?
Schedule never waives the statute. If time is truly critical, the honest tools are a properly supported proposal now, or leadership accepting the risk path with eyes open — not thin data.

scenarios.board_answer: This is a $14M sole-source action after the June 2026 cutover, so certified cost or pricing data is required — prior competition excepted the old action, not this one. I'd evaluate the commercial assertion on the $6M sub; if it holds, the sub is excepted from certification but I still need enough data to find its price fair and reasonable. Then price analysis plus element-by-element cost analysis with a real technical eval, weighted guidelines for profit, PNM and certificate at agreement — and the fiscal calendar doesn't change any of it.

coach.qtype: a pricing question — RFO 15.403 on what data you're owed, RFO 15.404 on the analysis the file needs.
coach.smes: your pricing office, DCMA for field pricing and rates, DCAA for audit, and Legal on defective-pricing exposure.
coach.rule: Price analysis always (RFO 15.404-1). Certified data only past the threshold with the RFO 15.403-2 CLAWM exceptions checked first — and no award without a documented fair-and-reasonable determination.

scenarios.ask: The prime says the subcontract is commercial and the prior competition covers the rest. What data are you owed, and how do you analyze this?
scenarios.script: This is a pricing question — RFO 15.403 on the data I'm owed, RFO 15.404 on the analysis the file needs. My help: my pricing office, DCMA for rates, DCAA if audit support fits, Legal on the exposure. The rules: this is a new $14M sole-source action after the June 2026 cutover, so certified cost or pricing data is required — the old competition excepted the old action, not this one. On the $6M subcontract, I evaluate the commercial assertion myself; if it holds, that excepts certification, not data — I still need enough to find the sub's price fair and reasonable. Then price analysis plus element-by-element cost analysis with a real technical evaluation, weighted guidelines on profit, and the certificate and PNM at agreement. The fiscal calendar changes none of it.

follow_ups.q: Recite the exceptions to certified cost or pricing data.
follow_ups.h: Five letters: CLAWM.
follow_ups.d: RFO 15.403-2 — CLAWM: Commercial products and services (including qualifying minor modifications); prices set by Law or regulation; Adequate price competition; a Waiver granted by the HCA; and commercial Modifications. Run the exceptions before demanding the certificate — most actions never need one. Here, none applies to the prime's $14M sole-source non-commercial action, so certification attaches.

follow_ups.q: What are the four proposal analysis types, and when does each apply?
follow_ups.h: Price always — then cost, technical, and profit.
follow_ups.d: Price analysis — always, every action (RFO 15.404-1): comparison of offers, history, catalogs, the IGCE. Cost analysis — element by element when certified data is required or realism must be judged: labor, materials, indirects, rates verified through DCMA. Technical analysis — engineers assessing hours, skill mix, BOMs, bases of estimate. Profit/fee analysis — DoD's weighted guidelines when certified data is required, with the statutory fee ceilings (15% R&D, 10% most cost-type, 6% A&E).

follow_ups.q: All five elements of defective pricing — go.
follow_ups.h: Data, timing, disclosure, reliance, effect.
follow_ups.d: (1) The information fits the definition of cost or pricing data; (2) accurate and complete data existed before the agreement on price; (3) it was not disclosed to the contracting officer; (4) the Government relied on the defective data in negotiations; (5) that reliance increased the contract price. All five must hold — intent is famously not an element. Remedy: price reduction plus interest, and profit on the delta.

follow_ups.q: What dollar thresholds bring in DCMA and DCAA?
follow_ups.h: Field pricing versus audit — two ladders.
follow_ups.d: DCMA field pricing assistance: over $2.5M fixed-price, over $10M cost-type (over $2.5M cost-type with system deficiencies). DCAA audits: over $10M fixed-price, over $100M cost-type. This $14M sole-source FPIF action sits squarely in DCMA field-pricing territory with DCAA audit available — and the $6M subcontract's rates ride the same support.

scenarios.scenario: A PM wants to award a $28M "FFP" contract for operating and continuously improving a legacy data-processing pipeline — the improvement work is "whatever the ops tempo surfaces, we can't predict it." The contractor proposed a 12% fee "to cover the unknowns," and offers to "convert to T&M whenever things get fuzzy." The contractor has never had a Government cost-type contract and its accounting system has never been reviewed.

facts.why: The improvement scope is genuinely unestimable — that half of the work can't carry FFP. Structure it: FFP the defined operations, and put the unpredictable work in a separately typed lane sized to its risk.
Padding fee to absorb risk is the FFP failure mode in miniature — price risk through structure (type, incentive, ceiling), not through fee.
T&M is a last resort with a D&F, ceiling, and exit plan — not a convenience valve. An open conversion promise is an invitation to never estimate anything.
Whatever cost-type or T&M lane emerges, the accounting-system gate comes first — that fact constrains the whole menu.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd split the requirement: FFP the well-defined operations, and for the unpredictable improvement work pick a type that matches its risk — which first means dealing with the accounting-system gate. Fee doesn't absorb risk, structure does; and T&M only enters with a D&F and an exit plan, not as a standing escape hatch.

coach.qtype: a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: who carries the cost risk, and why.
coach.smes: your pricing office, the PM on requirement certainty, and your reviewing chain for the D&F.
coach.rule: RFO Part 16 matches risk to definition: FFP when the work prices firmly; cost-type (approved accounting system + D&F) when it can't. Forcing FFP onto the unknowable is risk denial, not risk transfer — and E.O. 14402 makes other-than-FFP a justified decision (RFO 16.104).

scenarios.ask: The PM wants the $28M FFP award as proposed. What's your advice on the structure?
scenarios.script: This is a contract-type question — RFO Part 16: who carries the cost risk, and whether the structure matches the work. My help: my pricing office and the reviewing chain on the D&F. The rule: match type to requirement definition. So I'd split it: FFP the operations work — it's well-defined and priceable — and for the unpredictable improvement work, pick a type that matches genuine uncertainty, which first means confronting the accounting-system gate, because no adequate system means no cost-type award. And I'd name the fallacy out loud: fee doesn't absorb risk, structure does. A 12% fee on an FFP wrapper around unknowable work just buys a padded price. T&M only enters with a D&F and an exit plan — never as a standing escape hatch.

follow_ups.q: What factors drive contract-type selection?
follow_ups.h: Definition, estimate, risk, competition, systems, history.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 16: how well-defined the requirement is; how accurate the cost estimate can be; the technical risk; the competition available; whether the contractor has an adequate accounting system; and the acquisition history for similar work. The answers tell you how much cost risk the Government should retain versus transfer — type selection is a risk decision wearing a form number.

follow_ups.q: What gates must every cost-type contract clear?
follow_ups.h: A system and a signature.
follow_ups.d: An adequate contractor accounting system — because the Government pays incurred costs, the system that captures them must be trustworthy — and a D&F justifying the type. No system, no cost-type award, whatever the mission pressure. That's why this scenario's accounting-system question comes before any structure conversation.

follow_ups.q: If they push T&M for the improvement work — what does the D&F have to say?
follow_ups.h: Five findings, and approval scales with dollars and years.
follow_ups.d: A T&M D&F addresses: market research was conducted; it's genuinely impossible to estimate the extent or duration of the work; no other contract type is appropriate; the contract minimizes T&M use; and the steps that will reduce T&M on future requirements. Approval: COCO to $10M, SCO above, HCA for periods over three years. T&M is the careful exception — a ceiling, active surveillance, and an exit plan, never a standing convenience.

scenarios.scenario: Calibration-services MA-IDIQ, two holders: a large business at $7.1M of its $7.5M ceiling, and an SDVOSB at $2.6M of its ceiling, both minimums satisfied, three ordering years left. A $260K Phase II repair requirement arrives; the customer wants it awarded to the large business "as a logical follow-on to their Phase I win." The SDVOSB was rated technically acceptable in the Phase I competition. The large business's BD lead has already emailed you a draft SOW "to save time."

facts.why: The "logical follow-on" would nearly exhaust the large holder's ceiling with three years left — steering an order into a nearly-full ceiling is bad vehicle management even before fairness enters.

facts.fact: SDVOSB rated acceptable in Phase I
facts.why: A capable second holder guts "only one capable" and weakens "logical follow-on" — fair opportunity (or an order-level set-aside) is available and defensible.
A holder writing the order's SOW is a biased-ground-rules OCI in miniature — decline it, write our own, and note the contact in the file.
A $260K order competition between two holders costs days, not months — the time argument doesn't survive arithmetic.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd compete it between the holders — the SDVOSB proved capability in Phase I, so no exception honestly fits; and steering it would nearly max the large holder's ceiling anyway. The vendor-drafted SOW goes unused, and if the customer insists, the exception needs a D&A I don't think survives review.

coach.qtype: a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.505: every holder's real chance, or a documented exception.
coach.smes: the vehicle's PCO and ordering guide, the Competition Advocate for over-SAT D&As, and the ombudsman lane for holder complaints.
coach.rule: RFO 16.505 makes fair opportunity the default on multiple-award vehicles; exceptions ride a D&A up the same approval ladder as J&As, and consideration must be genuine — not rotation paperwork.

scenarios.ask: The customer wants this order steered to the large holder as a logical follow-on. What would you do?
scenarios.script: This is a fair-opportunity question — RFO 16.505. My help: the vehicle's ordering guide, my Small Business Professional, and the Competition Advocate if an exception were real. The default: every holder gets a genuine chance at every order. Walking the facts: the SDVOSB proved capability in Phase I, so 'only one capable' fails; a logical follow-on has to stand on continuity economics, not preference — and it weakens every time it's stacked on a sole-source original. Steering this also nearly maxes the large holder's ceiling, which is just bad vehicle management. So I'd compete it between the holders, the vendor-drafted SOW goes unused, and if the customer insists, I'd tell them plainly: the exception needs an RFO 16.505 D&A, and I don't believe this one survives review.

follow_ups.q: What are ALL the exceptions to fair opportunity under RFO 16.505?
follow_ups.h: Six — urgency, uniqueness, follow-on, minimum, statute, and a set-aside lane.
follow_ups.d: RFO 16.505: (1) unacceptable delay in meeting an urgent need; (2) only one awardee is capable — unique or highly specialized circumstances; (3) logical follow-on to an order already competed under fair opportunity — use with caution, especially stacked; (4) necessary to satisfy the minimum guarantee; (5) authorized or required by statute; (6) order-level small business set-aside — which needs no D&A. Recite all six cold; it's the 16.5 counterpart to the seven CICA exceptions.

follow_ups.q: What does an over-SAT exception require, and who approves it?
follow_ups.h: Same ladder as the J&A, different document.
follow_ups.d: A Determination and Approval — structured like a J&A, riding the same tiers: COCO to $900K, Competition Advocate to $20M, HPA/PEO to $90M ($150M DoD), SPE above — posted to SAM.gov (redacted) within 14 days, 30 for urgency. This $260K order sits below the SAT, so no D&A is required — but the fair-opportunity obligation itself never goes away; the file still shows genuine consideration.

follow_ups.q: What are the order-protest rules on this vehicle?
follow_ups.h: A dollar door and a growth door.
follow_ups.d: GAO hears task-order protests over $35M for DoD ($10M civilian) — or at ANY value where the protest alleges the order exceeds the scope, period, or ceiling of the underlying contract. Below those doors, the lane is the task-order ombudsman, who reviews whether holders got fair consideration and can recommend corrective action. A steered $260K order can't reach GAO — but the SDVOSB absolutely gets the ombudsman, which is why the consideration record matters at every dollar value.

scenarios.scenario: A depot-support contract's option two is due; notice date in 21 days. The COR's file: two quality escapes, both closed with corrective action, CPARS "satisfactory." The contractor emails: they'll "need a 9% price adjustment to keep performing" because of wage pressure — "or we'd understand a no-cost mutual walk-away." The PM says funding for the option year arrives in the new fiscal year, three weeks after the notice date.

facts.why: An option exercises at its priced terms — a contractor conditioning performance on a raise is refusing the option and inviting a negotiation. Exercise unilaterally at the option price, or don't; there's no "exercise at +9%."
The performance gate: documented, considered, and here probably passable — flags with completed corrective action are a judgment call to make on the record.

facts.fact: Funding arrives after the notice date
facts.why: Availability-of-funds mechanics exist for exactly this seam — align the exercise with the funds clause rather than obligating money that isn't there (the fiscal-law follow-up is coming).
That's the contractor negotiating against your leverage. The Government's alternatives — exercise, extend short, or recompete — get evaluated on their merits, not on the emailed menu.

scenarios.board_answer: The option exercises at its price or not at all — the 9% ask is a refusal dressed as a condition. I'd run the gates: performance is documented and arguably passes; the funding seam is handled through availability-of-funds mechanics; and if the contractor truly won't perform at the option price, my paths are a short extension while I recompete — with the record showing exactly why.

coach.qtype: an options question — RFO Part 17: the exercise gates, applied to today.
coach.smes: FM for funds, the COR and PM on performance and continuing need, and Legal if the notice window slipped.
coach.rule: Exercise only through the RFO Part 17 gates: funds, continuing need, most-advantageous check, SAM exclusions, performance considered — with timely written notice, or the unilateral right lapses into a bilateral negotiation.

scenarios.ask: Notice is due in 21 days and the contractor wants 9% to keep going. Do you exercise?
scenarios.script: This is an options question — the RFO Part 17 exercise gates, applied to today. My help: FM on funds, the COR's record, and Legal on the contractor's letter. The rule: an option exercises at its evaluated, awarded price or not at all — the unilateral right is exactly what we bought. The 9% demand is a refusal dressed as a condition. So I run the gates on the record: performance is documented — two escapes, closed, CPARS satisfactory — arguably passing; funds ride availability-of-funds mechanics across the fiscal seam; need continues. If the contractor truly won't perform at the option price, I don't negotiate the option — my paths are a short extension while I recompete, with the record showing exactly who declined what, and when.

follow_ups.q: Recite every gate you clear before exercising an option.
follow_ups.h: Seven checks, then a timely signature.
follow_ups.d: RFO Part 17: price still fair and reasonable — a fresh market look; funds available; the option serves an existing need and is the best method for it; the option was synopsized or is exempt; the contractor isn't excluded in SAM; performance has been considered; and written notice by the date in the contract. Miss the notice date and the unilateral right dies — continuation becomes a bilateral negotiation.

follow_ups.q: What duration limits cap a services structure?
follow_ups.h: Five, ten, and six months.
follow_ups.d: Service contracts: five years total, base plus all options (DFARS 217.204). DoD task and delivery order contracts: ten years without a Head of Agency determination, SPE approval beyond that. The extension-of-services clause adds at most six months — a transition bridge, not a strategy. And any period bought with the extension clause counts against the honest answer to 'why wasn't the recompete ready?'

follow_ups.q: The contractor flatly refuses to perform at the option price. What are your lawful paths?
follow_ups.h: You can't negotiate an option — but you can bridge and recompete.
follow_ups.d: An option exercises at its evaluated, awarded price or not at all — 'exercise plus 9%' is a new agreement, not an option, and it forfeits the competitive pricing the option preserved. Paths: exercise anyway if they're bluffing (refusal to perform an exercised option is anticipatory repudiation with T4D exposure); or don't exercise, use a short justified extension for continuity, and recompete immediately — with the record showing exactly who refused what. Either way, the refusal enters their performance record.

scenarios.scenario: September 12th. A PM arrives with a signed MIPR for $1.9M of current-year O&M to a civilian agency's assisted-acquisition shop for a "12-month analytics support task" — award expected "by December, they're backed up." The PM says the funds "are good because we're sending them before September 30th," and there's no interagency agreement on file yet, "but they say their standard one covers everything."

facts.why: Sending expiring funds cross-agency doesn't extend their life — the bona fide need and obligation rules follow the money. A December award of FY-expiring O&M for services starting then is the parking scheme fiscal lawyers feast on.

facts.fact: "Good because we send them before Sep 30"
facts.why: Transfer isn't obligation. The clock runs until a qualifying obligation exists — moving money to another agency's account doesn't stop it.
Assisted acquisition requires the signed agreement — roles, terms, fees — before performance. "Their standard one covers everything" is not an agreement in our file.
The best-procurement-approach D&F is required — and "they're backed up until December" is evidence against this being the best approach.

scenarios.board_answer: Three problems: the funds question — expiring O&M doesn't gain life by traveling, so a December award likely fails bona fide need; the missing interagency agreement, which must be signed before we proceed; and the D&F, which has to honestly conclude a backed-up shop is our best approach. As written, I'd pull the MIPR back and either buy it ourselves or fix all three on the record.
